reviewText: I bought this a few months ago.  We already owned theTolo Toys Rolling Shape Sorter- which I highly reccommend - but I've found that in our house it's best to own two of anything involving lots of small plastic bits (since generally speaking - if we own just one we will lose at least 1/2 the pieces, but if we own two - for whatever reason - we won't lose a single piece...frustrating).  Since the tolo one is a bit pricy & I figured he'd benefit from diversity I bought a different one...admittedly a cheaper one in comparison to others.  And I basically wasted my money...well - no - I bought a $10 bucket.The lid is not fixed - in any way - you can just lift it up at any given point...or if you knock it over the lid will come off as it literally just rests on top of the bucket.  This proves to be completely useless for a kid until they reach the age where they are actually more interested in specifically fitting shapes into the lid than simply figuring out what possible purposes this item could serve...and anything under 18mths is definitely not that age.  My son has no interest whatsoever in the lid or the shapes.  He loves his tolo sorter - sorts the pieces as intended & has undoubtedly learned the concept behind sorting from that toy.  This...is used as a bucket.  He's great at taking the pieces out - by either the quick & easy dump method or the meticulous piece-by-piece method - but ultimately - he does that with the other bins we have for his toys - and at least then he'll occasionally find something that interests him in the process...and I already have a set of jumbo colored/shaped buttons I use to teach him colors & shapes so I can't really think of any other use for the plastic pieces.  They seem to simply be one more thing I get to pick up since he sees them the same way I do - just as being in the way...they're currently kept in a ziplock bag since I can't stand picking them up anymore.  Same with the lid - I tried using that on its own & putting the pieces in with the lid on the ground - he had no interest in this - ever (with or without me involved).Ultimately...I'm not quite sure why fisher-price would label this as a Basic Baby - since if it's designed for the "basic baby" stage the lid needs to be attached (or lock on in some way).  But it's a great bucket...
summary: It's a great bucket...but a useless sorter...

reviewText: My son received this as a gift to go with hisMelissa & Doug Deluxe Standing Easel, and my son loves it. Comes with seven items:1) Washable paint in four colors: red, blue, yellow, green...my son has learned how to mix colors for orange and purple...and the paint is washable but you still might want to purchase aMelissa and Doug Artist's Smock.2) Paper roll is nice, but kind of thin...depending on how your child paints, it may soak through a little.3) Dry-erase marker in blue; I bought an Expo Low Odor Dry Erase Marker Set so my son would have different colors, but the one that comes with the set works great & wipes off easily.4) Felt eraser. We use this one for the chalkboard side of his easel, and I bought another eraser for the dry-erase side of the easel.5) The spill-proof cups are awesome. The lids screw off so you can pour the paint in, and they have flip tops that can be open while in use. There is a hole under the flip lid that accomodates the paint brush, and the area around the hole slants downwards so any run-off slides back into the cup and not over the edge.6) The four paintbrushes come in red, blue, yellow, and green -- helps a child keep the colors from getting messy.7) The chalk is awesome, but not sure why they have black chalk in the set -- you can't even see it on a green board. The chalk goes on and wipes off easy enough. The design makes it easier to hold, especially for littles ones learning how to hold a writing instrument correctly.I wish the set came with two erasers, and more than one dry-erase marker, but otherwise this is a perfect set.

reviewText: This is a cool "little" toy (it's actually not all that little, being the perfect size for a 5 year-old to play with). It has a decent assortment of interchangeable parts that give little minds some fun playing options. The missile-cannon is a fun addition, but obviously requires supervision to make sure ye olde eyes remain intact. The articulation is fairly robust, but not something that leads to a situation where a child twists the legs behind the head (and can't get them back to the correct position). The chest "armor" add-on is a bit annoying, however (this is where it loses a star). It works very much like a tiny belt, requiring one end to be threaded through a clasp on the other, then a bit of finagling to get things to stay in place (for about 10s, before they pop back out). Eventually, we just tossed the rubber armor (which meant we lost the missile pods, but it just wasn't worth the hassle). We don't have any other toys from this line, so can't comment on using parts from other heroes, but if the switching back and forth on Iron Man is any indication, it works extremely well. All told, this is an enjoyable toy, and with the full line, I'm sure Hydra is quaking in the boots as they contemplate the super hero possibilities.PS The gun comment in the title is a bit of a throwaway line, but seriously, has Iron Man ever used a gun (when he was Iron Man)? Just seems like an odd inclusion. Now an ridiculously oversized beam cannon? Yeah. :)

reviewText: This is another winner from Ravensburger! Unlike other electronic circuit building toys, this kit has dedicated components for each of the 8 different gadgets kids can build from this kit (except the 9V battery connector - see below). In addition, unlike the other kits where you simply connect wires from specific point to another, here you are building the circuit yourselves using resistors, capacitors, wire connectors etc.The kit comes with all the required components including a wire cutter and stripper tool! The instructions booklet has very good details about each component e.g. what a resistor does and why it is necessary in a circuit etc. This provides excellent educational value (especially for middle school aged kids). For each gadget, there is a printed cardboard circuit board that guides connections. You start by collecting the components and cut and strip the necessary length wires. Then you build the circuit as instructed using those components. The brass connectors are easy to use and hold the components fairly well. For gadgets such as flashlight and burglar alarm, there is a cardboard outer box that hides the circuit board (this is fairly thin cardboard and could have been a bit more thick).One caveat is that the kit provides only one 9V battery connector and therefore, you cannot build and use multiple gadgets in parallel. The kit does not provide the battery as well - so make sure you get a 9V battery before starting. While the box appears too big for the components in the kit, it is large enough to allow storing the built gadgets inside safely which is good. I would like to see a printed ruler to measure the wires before cutting. They could simply print it in the instruction booklet or include is as a component.
summary: Lets kids build some usable electronic gadgets - additional battery connectors would help!
filteredReviewText: This is another winner from Ravensburger! Unlike other electronic circuit building toys, this kit has dedicated components for each of the 8 different gadgets kids can build from this kit (except the 9V battery connector - see below). In addition, unlike the other kits where you simply connect wires from specific point to another, here you are building the circuit yourselves using resistors, capacitors, wire connectors etc.The kit comes with all the required components including a wire cutter and stripper tool! The instructions booklet has very good details about each component e.g. what a resistor does and why it is necessary in a circuit etc. This provides excellent educational value (especially for middle school aged kids). Then you build the circuit as instructed using those components. The brass connectors are easy to use and hold the components fairly well. For gadgets such as flashlight and burglar alarm, there is a cardboard outer box that hides the circuit board (this is fairly thin cardboard and could have been a bit more thick).One caveat is that the kit provides only one 9V battery connector and therefore, you cannot build and use multiple gadgets in parallel. The kit does not provide the battery as well - so make sure you get a 9V battery before starting. While the box appears too big for the components in the kit, it is large enough to allow storing the built gadgets inside safely which is good. I would like to see a printed ruler to measure the wires before cutting.

reviewText: We don't play board games all that often, but every couple weeks we sit around a table, maybe invite the neighbors, get some snacks and play.  Last time we played this one a couple times and it was a lot of fun guessing and learning about body part and functions - described in such a way as to balance the "gross factor" with the "wow!" factor.  My older kids (and the adults) knew a lot of the answers, but the younger ones had fun learning.  I'd say that likely the best place for this game would be in the science classroom.  Used as a game for breaking up the routine - even if you just used the trivia cards without playing the game, and gave out rewards or points for correct answers - this would be a lot of fun.  As a standard move around the board game I expect it will get boring after the novelty wears off, and after we've encountered most of the questions.

reviewText: This is an absolutely ADORABLE gift for a new baby, or one that's in the crawling phase.  Maybe even a 1st birthday gift for a new walker.  Any adult who receives this gift will find it incredibly cute.  It's MUCH softer than you would expect a mechanical to toy to be (it's a Gund!), and is quite entertaining to listen to and watch.On the other hand, if you're a parent, it might not be the best toy to buy for *your* baby.  Why?  My 8-month old daughter doesn't actually crawl after it.  She doesn't tap it.  She just watches - in amazement - for 30 seconds and then crawls off, sometimes before it's done walking.  I'm not sure that it's really worth it for just that.Her 3-year old big brother does enjoy tapping it and making it crawl, so it's sort of a game they can play together...  but this toy isn't cheap, and I have to imagine there might be better places for my dollars to go.Let me know if your little ones behave differently.  I'll certainly update this review if my little girl starts to crawl after it more, or if I see other babies react differently.

reviewText: I was reluctant to get this for my two boys, 3 and 4 1/2, after reading several less than stellar reviews.  I decided to bite the bullet and try it out after watching several youtube videos reviewing it.  I have to say that my kids and I love it!  The initial set up was kind of annoying, but as long as you have a good internet connection, the downloading of books and software isn't that big of a deal.  Once downloaded, my kids took off.  Even my 3 year old enjoys playing with it.  He doesn't "read" as much as push the games that are on nearly every page, but my 4 year old reads and plays the games.The only negative complaint I have about this product is the amount of memory storage.  I think it can hold 10 books, which is pretty good, but the product line has A TON of books and games.  I know eventually I will have to take things off to accommodate for more books.As far as battery life, I can't say just yet.  My kids have had it almost a week and are still going strong, but time will tell.  I monitor their use, so I am always aware of when they stop playing so that I can remind them to turn it off.  They are now remembering to turn it off as soon as they are done, and I am sure this helps the battery life.If you don't like downloading software or you have little or no internet connection, don't get this product.  If you aren't scared of a little bit of software and have a strong internet connection, your children will most likely enjoy this fun, educational toy.

reviewText: I received this for a Christmas present, I actually had it on my list because I thought it would be a fun exploration into flying RC vehicles and not cost a fortune to do so.When I opened it I was initially impressed with what I saw. It was already assembled and looks good. I charged it up with the supplied charger and put the AA batteries it requires into the handset.Per the directions you are suppose to fully throttle up, then all the way down before turning the helicopter on, make sure you do this. It ensures the zero and full throttle ranges are set. Speaking of instructions, they are bad, really bad, about what you would expect from an auto-translated original so expect poor English.On to the flight test... I placed it on a wide open flat surface, the dinning room table. Per the advice of other reviews I slowly ramped up power until the helicopter started to rotate on the table. I then adjusted the trim until the rotation stopped. This will make the helicopter stay pointing in one direction when in flight instead of rotating around in a circle.With that set, I upped the power to take off ... except it never happened. At full power it looked like it was trying to take off, but all it would accomplish is tipping over onto its side for an abrupt stop. Okay, so maybe something's off, instead I tried holding it in my hand and going to full throttle, then letting go. All I got was a slow descent to the floor, where it touched, then tipped over like on the table. I tried turning everything off, then trying the full throttle, to zero throttle adjustment again, powered up the helicopter ... and got the same results.I never was able to get this guy to fly after several attempts. In addition, on my second attempt to charge it, the USB portion of the charger broke apart, not really broke but just came apart. It is just a USB connector with two wires soldered onto the contacts of the connector, one of the wires unsoldered so it couldn't simply be 'snapped' back together. I could of fixed it myself, but with the fact that I couldn't get it flying in the first place I decided just to return it.You may or may not have luck with this. Several people obviously got it working well so either I missed something in the bad directions, or my unit was defective.

reviewText: This LeapFrog Disney Learning Game is great! Although the graphics are obviously basic and retro compared with today's console systems, Phineas and Ferb's "tricked out" ride and adventures in acquiring the ultimate water balloon launcher make this video game a winner. I don't think my son really understands the science, reasoning or engineering components of the game, but he was good at the basic math throughout the game and was good at matching geometric patterns.  Although he does not understand anything about conductivity and insulation, he does remember which objects go where in order to generate power and progress through the game (therefore, I think this game can sharpen your child's short term memory skills).  This LeapFrog offering has good educational value yet is also fun to play.

reviewText: Hasbro's Playskool Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset is recommended for children 18 months and up. My granddaughter is 27 months old and she loves it. It was easy to unbox and assemble and assembly literally took less than 2 minutes (I knew beforehand from looking at Hasbro's product page to have 3 AA batteries ready as they are required but not included, and because I always keep my Leatherman multi-tool handy I had a Phillips head screwdriver - also required for assembly - ready to go). My granddaughter took to the Playset immediately (something that I can't say about all the toys I've given her and that she otherwise gets), letting out a delighted sounding "Wheeeee!" every time one of the Weebles figures went down the slide. She first had to learn that she had to turn a crank in order to elevate the Weebles figures up the escalator to the top of the spiraling slide, and she had to figure out which way to turn the crank. That only took moments, and once she got the hang of it, she became absorbed in playing with the Weebles Playset. In addition to bringing the happy-faced figures up the escalator and sending them down the curvy slide, one can play hide-and-seek with them (there's a hiding space inside the tree), and one can put the egg-shaped figures on the wobbly tree-house deck. There is lots of motion with this toy to keep a child absorbed.Sometimes after meals and naps she says, "Weebles!" whereupon she RUNS to the Playset. She often dances to the music that plays to "reward" a Weebles figure after it goes down the slide. Speaking of the music, that and the other sounds of the Playskool Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset, such as the crank being turned, is not so loud as to be annoying when compared to some other toys (e.g., a couple of Leap Frog brand toys). My granddaughter's parents, her "nana" (my son-in-law's mom) and I agree on this, though the volume and kind of toy noise a given adult may find overly loud and/or annoying is obviously subjective. This seems to be one toy that will have staying power, and in 16 months my granddaughter's baby brother will be old enough to play with it!Good quality toy; an easy 5 stars and high recommendation. (You can watch a 46-seconds long professionally-made video review of Hasbro's Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset at timetoplaymag.)

reviewText: Let me start off with the positives-- the tops included in this set (two five piece tops) are wicked cool.  Those things will spin for very long periods of time if you spin them on a flat surface.  They also have a nice weight to them.  They look like solid products that any boy or girl would want on hand for those 'down times' when they just want to see something spin!  The idea is neat.  It would be awesome to actually figure out how to get the tops to do more than, say, land in the bottom of the dome, but that must take a lot of practice, from what I can see!The cons? reviewText: We have a closet full of games that get pulled out occasionally, but since we received Make n Break they're all just gathering dust. This game is SO. MUCH. FUN!My kids read the directions and in five minutes had it set up and were playing on their own. It comes with about 10 differently colored rectangular building blocks, a stack of cards, a timer, and cardboard chips with point values on them. Easy set up, easy clean up, which is always a bonus.You simply roll the dice to see how long your turn will be, set the timer to that amount, and then when the time starts you flip over the top card and attempt to build the structure pictured on the card. Sometimes they are easy, with only three blocks, and sometimes they are towers of balancing craziness that send the builder into a frenzy trying to complete it. If you finish the first card and don't make any mistakes (the other players are watching carefully to make sure) you knock it all down and grab another card and build what's on it, continuing until the time runs out. However many cards you complete gives you your points for the round and you get a token that represents how many points you have. Whoever has the most points at the end of four rounds wins.The instructions say that a game is four rounds, but you could set any number of rounds that you wish. The instructions also say it's for 2-4 players, but I see no reason why you couldn't play with as many people as you want. We frequently play with 5 to 6 people and it just makes the game last a little longer. And lastly, the instructions say it's for ages 8 and up, but my 5-year-old plays happily with us and we just give him a little handicap on the points. It's rare to find a game that adults and kindergarteners can equally enjoy, but Make n'Break does it.My only complaint is that the crash of pushing over the tower of blocks is so loud my husband and I can't have Make 'N' Break tournaments after the kids are in bed.
summary: Easy to learn, quick to play, and lots of fun

reviewText: In a recent review, I complained about the lack of sturdiness of modern toys.  However, this play house is sturdy and seems as though it would provide many years of play to several generations of children.  The play house is also pretty, and large enough that you could stuff a lot of things into it.The only complaint I have about this play house is the lack of pirate-related stuff to go into it.  You do get some blocky figures and cannons, but no pirate treasure, no steering wheel, no little pirate swords, or anything similar.  I suppose that if you were trying to give this play house to a small child, the lack of small parts could be an advantage.  However, if I were a small child, I would be asking mom and dad for stuff to go into my pirate play house.If you are looking for a play house for a small boy or girl, this play house is a winner from the perspective that it seems like it would take a lot of abuse.  On the flip side, it includes very few features, so you end up populating the play house with other toys you have.  This play house begs for some sort of add on feature or set(s) that allow a child to expand play possibilities.Enjoy!

reviewText: The Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm is a toy your little one will probably love.  The colorful barn has stall/stable doors that open and close; a chicken in the hayloft; and cute animals and Little People with which your child can imagine vaious scenarios.  The barn complex is well made; it has smooth seams and no sharp edges.  The silo serves as a storage chamber for the multiple figures and snaps into the main barn structure to produce a more compact footprint. A red tractor is the sole piece of farm equipment included in the Fisher-Price Animal Sounds Farm.The animals included in the Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm are well made.  Each one has rounded edges and no visible seams.  The animals are not proportionally sized; the goat is the same size as the horse, etc.The animal sounds are created by opening and closing doors or sliding the hayloft chicken.  There is no discrete placing of an animal in a specific spot to produce its sound.  For example, it is not necessary to place the horse in the stall where opening the door produces a "neigh" - one simply must open and close the stall door.  This defeats the "learning" aspect of the Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm.  For this reason, I prefer the Fisher-Price Little People A to Z Learning Zoo.To some, there is an even more detrimental feature of the Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm.  Once younger children discover all it takes is repeated opening and closing of doors or moving the hayloft chicken from side-to-side to create a cacophony of barnyard noises, all hope for peace is lost...  Little ones find absolute delight in generating these noises which can rapidly become annoying and require removal of the batteries to stop.The Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm is a fun toy for younger children.  Our grandson received one for his second birthday - the joyful look on his face when he opened it was heartwarming.  He has played with "Farmer Joe" and the barnyard every day since receiving it.I rated the Fisher-Price Little People Animal Sounds Farm as a 4-star toy because of its limited learning potential and because it has a fairly short playlife since older children may find it boring.  It received the 4 stars, instead of 3, because my grandson loves it and plays with it regularly.

reviewText: I've bought several set of Fisher Price Little People over the years as gifts, and never been disappointed.  I thought this gift would be a home run since it was Little People, animals and a train, but in this instance it wasn't as big of a hit as I thought it would be.I didn't realize when I bought it that it is really meant to be a companion piece to the larger Zoo Talkers set.  The quality of the set is Fisher Price, so it's cute, kids love the animals, the sounds and the colors, it's fairly durable and can withstand a lot of use, but unfortunately not all of the pieces make the noises like I thought they would since they were all sold together as a set.  A big disappointment since the little one that I bought it for doesn't have the larger Zoo Talker set. I think this is basically a way for the toy manufacturer to sell more of both sets.  Since the Zoo Talkers set doesn't have these animals included in the train set, but not all of the animals in the train set will work and make the sounds unless you have the larger Zoo set.  I don't like that.  I think that every piece sold with the set should work with the set without having to purchase another set to get them to work.  This may be a way for them to try and sell more of everything, but instead it has made me a bit wary of buying more from them without checking online reviews first.If you are looking for just a train, this might be fine but a little overpriced for what it does.  If you have the larger Zoo Talkers set, I think you will probably really love it, but if you don't you may want to reconsider a different Little People set (like maybe the Farm).

reviewText: This is a pretty good way to introduce preschoolers to the exciting world of board games. There are four different games in the box, each pretty simple to play. The games require no reading skills, just the ability to match colors. The games included are as follows:"The Bird's Nest" - This one is my daughter's favorite of the four games. Players move up the colored path in the various birds' nests in an attempt to be the first to reach the eggs that are nestled in the center of the nest. This game has two variations of play, one easy variant and one easier variant for those children who get frustrated easily."Garden Party" - Each player has a flower bed and throws the colored die to determine which color flower that player will receive in his/her garden. The first player to collect one flower of each color wins the game."King of the Castle" - For moms and dads who are already familiar with children's board games, this game has a slight "Candyland" flavor to it, except with a castle theme instead of a candy one. Players throw the colored die and move their piece to the corresponding colored space. When a player throws the color white, that player picks a card and moves to the space with the corresponding picture on it. Here is an opportunity for a child to be forced to move backwards, if the picture on the card happens to be located behind the player who drew the card. reviewText: This is visually a very attractive toy for a young person. It was a gift for my 5 year old who loves the sea. Upon receiving it, he was thrilled, however:1) The toy is primarily a ship meant to harpoon sharks. Given large sharks are not typically used for food, it seemed a bit gratuitous. It also recalled images of whaling, of which we are not advocates. In response, I opened the package and removed the harpoon and the carcass holder. I also presented it without the box so that he wouldn't be influenced to play in the way that was shown (hunting the shark, shark eating divers, etc.). Even after playing for many weeks with the toy, this has not become the mode of play for my son so I am glad to have removed the images.2) It doesn't click together firmly. The wheels don't stay on if pushed firmly, the side boats are a bit tricky to attach. It can't be reliably picked up from anywhere but the bottom.3) I am not sure why there are two or three sets of fasteners, which reduce flexibility. For example, there are small boats that attach to the side. But they cannot attach directly because the fittings on the sides of the large and small boat are both the same gender. One needs an intermediate piece that has the opposite gender on both sides to make it work. If this were lego, you could likely attach the pieces however you like. Similarly, attaching the crane and other components can only be done in some orientations and not in others because the fastners are different. What you can make is limited.4) It doesn't float well. The instructions say you need to have the smaller boats attached for stability, which is true, but they come off easily.Overall my son enjoys it, but it doesn't feel or behave like a quality toy.

reviewText: There are a lot of really nice things about this toy: in particular, it does a very good job of providing an interactive real-world playset that can compete with iPad app for my son's attention.  It's a bit sad to say, but at this point, that's my metric.  If a toy can keep my 3-year old son from the TV or the iPad, I like it.  The more it keeps him away from the screens, the more I like it!My son loves having the police car go to the donut shop and hearing the thick New York City (Brooklyn, really, I think) accents.  The only flip side is that the sound effects are somewhat limited and have the potential to get repetitive after a while, but additional playsets are available to expand the city.In order to get the sounds to work, the kids actually have to park the little vehicles in the correct grooves.  That may be a bit tough for the younger kids and might be why the minimum recommended age is 4.Speaking of the little vehicles, my only issue with this is that we have to be very careful around my eight month old daughter. reviewText: For the price, I actually prefer this Nerf Super Soaker over the other more expensive one I received last week. reviewText: The LeapFrog LeapReader Writing Workbook teaches numbers and some basic reading and math skills.  It requires using theLeapFrog LeapReader Reading and Writing System, which is an electronic pen with audio.  It is indeed part of a system, and requires online registration, but is a different system from the LeapFrog TAG reading system, even though it looks somewhat similar.  If you are buying this as a gift, talk to the parent first, to make sure it is compatible.  There are over 150 different activity books available for the system.This book is fun to use, but the children will require some adult assistance.  The educational value is very good, with an emphasis on actually writing numbers.  Remember how hard it was to make a good-looking "8" or "5"?  This provides a template and immediate feedback based on the actual strokes.  A couple of dozen practice pages are included.
summary: Modern system for learning basic literacy skills

reviewText: I ordered this puzzle ball for my nearly 6 year old son to place in his room when it was completed.  Straight out of the package my two daughters aged 8 & 9 fought over placing the pieces around the dome.  The puzzle ball is a lot smaller then the image has you believing.  It is about 8 inches high and about 14 in diameter.  The puzzle pieces are hard formed plastic and there is no fear of being bent, nor are they very flexible; if anything they have a tiny bit of flexibility.  The pieces fit together a tad snugly which assures that your 'puzzle ball' will not come apart after you have placed it for display.  Within the box, you will find two yellow rings that will begin your puzzle at the equator.  There is only one plastic half dome piece to work on.  After you have completed one half you then move onto the other half.  Finally you are able to snap both halves together and form a WHOLE (fraction lesson at its finest!).  The ball is not bouncy, so please do not throw around or at anything.  You will break the ball and whatever you choose to chuck it at.Did they like it?  Well, the girls loved it and fought over the pieces.  I actually sat and helped and feel a bit dumb because it took us 15 minutes to complete both sides.  I really believed that for a 40 piece puzzle this would be a breeze for my 5 year old.  It wasn't.  My eldest (nearly 10) had to really study the pieces and that is when I would swoop in and help them along.  The child that this puzzle was intended for was distracted with the yellow bands with the star, moon etc. shapes on it.  He became exasperated at times because the blues would confuse him.  I do believe that we all struggled a bit because it was the first time that we have attempted to put together a puzzle ball.Highly recommend for beginners with help from an adult or older sibling.  I do believe the age recommendation should be raised to 6+.  Lastly, I would love it if Ravensburger would include a small plastic stand that could properly display the child's effort.  I deducted a star for that very reason.

reviewText: The 4 First Games Combo Pack is a box that contains four games. The box includes two 2-sided game boards - one on each side of the two boards. All the pieces are bright, colorful and of good quality.The games are King of the Castle, Tasty Bones, Garden Party and the Bird's nest.King of the Castle:This one is the best out of the four and our favorite. It's a lot like Candy Land. Same principle as Candy Land but you primarily use a die to move around the board. You also must land on the last space color exactly to win. Chance cards send you all over the board, backwards and forwards. Teaches and reinforces color, following directions, and taking turns.Tasty Bones:This one is a little complicated and our least favorite. You start by having to roll a certain color to get started and this can take a while. You roll the die and move left to right or up and down to the nearest square on the board of the color that you just rolled. The rules don't specify what to do if there isn't that color available in the rows you to need to move to so we just skipped a turn. You could also just roll again. It was really kind of boring and pointless so we just quit playing this one.Garden Party:A little fun. You roll the die and try to get one of each color flower to "plant" in your garden. First one to plant their garden wins. No much to the game so does not take long to play and not particularly that great or fun of a game either.The Bird's Nest:The kids had fun on this one just rooting for which color would come up.You must roll your die in a certain order to move your game piece. It takes a while to do this especially with young children who aren't great die throwers. You can change the rules and just move to whatever color you roll for younger players. We also changed the rules and let a player keep rolling if he did roll the right color instead of just taking turns. We also kept playing after someone won to see who would be next to make it to the "nest".Overall, nice gift set but I would probably skip it and just get Candy Land.

reviewText: The premise of this game is to guess what picture is over your head.  The picture is visible to everyone else but you.  In a way, this game reminds me of something called "Indian Poker", where everyone but you sees your card.Anyway, the idea behind this game is good, it's like a 20 questions, where you ask questions and people can say "yes/no".  The availability of the picture makes it so that a whole group can participate, versus one-on-one.However, here's where the hangups go.  The timer is for 45 seconds.  Consider that the average question takes about 5-10 seconds between asking and answering, we're talking about 5-10 questions before time's up.  We tried a house rule of flipping the timer an extra time (for a total of a minute and a half), but we still can't figure out the item in time!  I think the issue has to do with the timer, it messes with your head, and the questions you ask become scattered.  Perhaps if we had a new house rule and had a limited number of questions instead of relying on a set time, the game may work.  This may be especially useful when you have a diverse number of ages (young kids versus teens and adults).Also, there aren't that many cards.  I suppose we can create our own cards, but for this size game, you would think that the manufacturer would bother to give you a few more.  I'd see a cranium game, and they'd throw in about 300-500 examples.  For this game?  Not even 100.Based on the number of stars for other reviewers, I'm guessing that I'm in the minority, but I just can't love this game.  Again, great concept, but hard to play.Overall, okay game.  Could have easily been a 4 or 5 star game if they thought it through, gave game variations (like number of guesses), and gave more cards.UPDATE - 06/22/11So, it's been over half a year since we've received this item, and I must admit, the kids and wife still play it once in a while.  So while I don't love this game, it's still considered a keeper!

reviewText: This Nano Super Vert Crash Set gets a big No as far as playability goes. The teensy 1 inch cars are cute, but totally useless on or off the track. I hope X Concepts redesigns these race tracks so the cars stay on for the ride and make them so an actual race between 2 cars can go on, which is the best part of racing. With a better design, this Nano Set could have earned 5 Stars, instead of 1.

reviewText: This was probably the most confused that I've been with a new game...the number of symbols to learn is rather daunting at first, and it felt like I was flying blind in the first play through. Thankfully I played the game again after studying the symbol tip sheet, and my second game was a very different and satisfying experience. It's amazing to me that so much strategic complexity can be packed into a half-hour game.The game mechanic of getting seven cards to start each age, picking one, and then passing the remaining cards to your neighbor was a little odd to me at first but it works well for the game. Also given the name 7 Wonders I figured that building your wonder would be the largest part of the game and difficult to do but neither was the case. Your wonder is basically just another of seven total ways to score victory points, which is fine too...it is fun having that many options.All of the game components are beautiful. reviewText: My 4 year old autistic son loves this toy, but it takes a lot of work and supervision to help him enjoy it.  It has been great as far as getting my son to participate and interact with us.  He calls out the colors of the "butterflies" as they come out, he picks them up and puts them back in, he asks us to "turn it on" etc.  The problem stems from the way it absolutely drains batteries and the long plastic snout that the butterflies float through.  Because the snout folds closed, you have to manipulate it every time you start it, or the butterflies will never come out.  Sometimes the butterflies just hang out in the tube, so even my son knows how to tap it to get them to pop out.  And, it turns into a very expensive toy when you have to replace the 4 C batteries all the time.  We always use Energizer or Duracell, which are not cheap/weak batteries.  And, because I'm participating with my son every time, I make sure to turn it off as soon as possible to save battery life.I saw that another reviewer mentioned cutting the snout shorter, which I have thought of doing.  That might save some battery life, because the butterflies will spit out faster and you can turn it off more quickly.Also, we have not used the nets, but I haven't seen them as being dangerous.  They provide 4 nets (green, red, yellow, blue), but there are only 3 colors of butterflies (green, red, yellow).  I don't understand why there is a blue net, but perhaps it's in the directions I haven't read.Overall, I'd only suggest it to those parents who are willing/able to play with their kids every time they use it and can afford a lot of expensive batteries.

reviewText: My 2 year old daughter and 5 year old nieces absolutely love this toy! The playset comes with a pretty Cinderella figure, the carriage that has molds built into it, and 3 jars of Playdoh. We love that the carriage has molds you can press the Playdoh into to make the fairy god mother, her dress skirt, Jaq, Gus, birds, and a pumpkin. The Playdoh presses easily into them and comes out easily as well without ruining the mold you just made and it's easy to peel away the excess Playdoh around it. Her favorite is that the wheels of the carriage have brick imprints and Cinderella's slipper to make a stunning walkway for Cinderella to walk on. The top of the carriage is really neat that you can press it down and make pumpkin vines. The carriage itself is gorgeous and colorful and doubles as a working rolling carriage for Cinderella to ride in as well as for making the molds.The plastic carriage is thickly made and very durable to handle even rough play from younger kids. My daughter also likes to reenact the story with the molded figures and so it can be used for dramatic play as well. She also uses her other Disney Princess figurines to interact with Cinderella, though we don't put Playdoh on them.I love the creativity and old school fun this toy offers without any ritzy technology like most toys these days.The only downside to this toy is that it's hard to clean the Playdoh out of the vine press, but that's to be expected. It would've been nice to have a cutting tool included too. Overall, this is a big hit in our house and well worth the price, plus you can buy more Playdoh colors to go with this!

reviewText: I am a big fan of Walt Disney cartoons.  My girlfriend, Tammy, isn't.  However, we both had some fun playing the World of Disney Eye Found it Board Game.  It was exciting to hustle looking for hidden objects while the sands of time quickly vanished.  We had to be physically quick while using our intelligence, creativity, and memory.Both of us are fifty.  My eyesight, thankfully, is still approximately 20/20.  Tammy had more difficulty locating small objects.  I told her the next time we play we're using my magnifying glasses.  The board is very long, six feet, but it is also very narrow.  The drawings are very small.  Also, it is best to play this game on a carpeted floor.  My knees began hurting after playing it on Tammy's hard wooden floor.  I had to get a pillow to sit my knees on.I'm not a team player.  I think the game would have been more exciting if we were playing against each other rather than working as a team.  However, my biggest problem with the game is a lack of a good timer.  When a Search for hidden items begins, one of the players needs to turn over the sand timer.  When the sand runs out, the Search ends.  However, if all the players are diligently searching, who is watching the sand timer?  While Tammy and I searched, one of us, when we remembered, would glance over at the timer to see if all the sand had fallen.  Sometimes, we'd become so involved that we'd forget to look.The game would have been more fun if there had been a battery-operated timer that buzzes, alarms, chimes, etc., when the Search time has ended.  This wouldn't add much expense to the game.  However, it would add a lot more fun. reviewText: LeapFrog LeapReader Reading and Writing System is the new Upgraded version of the very popular Tag Reading system. If you have never tried or owned a Tag Reader system it's basically a touch based sensor system to help you child with word recognition, comprehension and of course reading.The upgraded Leapreader comes with some great new features including the ability to write/trace letters and words, an Audio player for music and Trivia games as well as mini-games within the books themselves.  The Leapreader is also backwards compatible with 150+ tag books and of course Leapfrog have released exclusive books and Writing Workbooks that work only/exclusively with the Leapreader itself.My 6yr old daughter really enjoys using this and it has helped her tremendously with her reading and word comprehension skills. I would definitely recommend this to any parent of a young child whose in the early stages of learning how to read or a reading beginner.

reviewText: Our family members love board games. After our Thanksgiving dinner, we played TAPPLE for the 1st time. The youngest player was a 7 year old. Everyone else were adults. The only concession to the 7 year old's age was that when she played we used the side of the cards with the easier topics ("Pizza toppings", "Ice cream flavors"). When she wandered off we played with the more difficult side of the cards("7-letter words", "Cosmetics & toiletries"). The game has all of the alphabet, with the exception of Q, U, V, X, Y, Z on keys that can be pressed down. When you pick a card you must announce the topic, push the timer button & come up with a word that fits the description with 10 seconds. You push down the letter that corresponds with the 1st letter of your word. Once a letter is used, it can't be used again during that game. The next person has 10 seconds to try to come up with a word that matches the same topic.The Pros: #1 The game is fun. It's easy to learn. Because there are 2 levels of cards, young players can join in the fun. There is a neat little compartment on the bottom of the wheel where the cards can be stored which makes the game very compact & portable. Each round goes rather quickly. If you don't have all day to build hotels on Park Place, you can still play TAPPLE.The Cons: The ticking of the darn timer is too loud. It makes me feel pressured, which is probably what its intended to do. :)I
summary: If you can think while a timer ticks, I recommend TAPPLE

reviewText: We tried this out tonight with another couple that likes board games, and we all had a good time. There is a decent amount of strategy and cut-throat play, but enough "luck of the draw" so that everyone has a chance to win, not just the best strategic thinkers. We played three games with three different winners.The game board and pieces are sturdy. The double deck of playing cards are decidedly on the cheap side. They'd have done better to just throw a couple of coated Bicycle decks into the box and forget trying to print their own. We were impressed that after you remove the four sets of pieces from the "tear open" bags, there were four pressure seal baggies to separate them into for storage.The rules as written are terrible. Like so many game rules these days, they have at least a couple of unintelligible sentences and ambiguities. We basically got the sense of what they intended and decided on our own house rules to cover the ambiguities. Evidently writing clear, concise rules is a lost art. It did give us a laugh making a joke that in an 8+ game, we four adults were unclear what they were trying to tell us in a couple of places.In our game, we played that diagonals are OK for the winning pathway. If you play by the "rules" that pieces forming your winning path must be adjacent on the sides and not diagonally, any particular game might last hours. It isn't fascinating enough for that sort of time investment.However, the four of us did enjoy the game and will probably play it again as a group.Recommended.

reviewText: The tie-in between play-dough and princesses is a stretch... you can make a mold of a prince using playdough, and it comes with three princess figurines (that don't have really anything to do with play-dough).  Each of the three princesses has a door in the castle they can be stored in, and the fourth door is the "prince mold".  There are a few other molds for things like flowers and teapots, and the only other play-dough related gimmick is the Rapunzel hair up at the top tower (you push play-dough in and it makes "hair" when you squeeze it back out).  Still, it's play-dough, which is always fun and stimulates the kid's imagination.  My six-year-old plays with the castle and the play-dough separately, though, so I really think of this as two different toys bundled together.

reviewText: Let me start by saying that our 4 year old loves to build things.  He loves blocks, magnatiles, legos--you name it.  BUT, he does not like to build alone.  One amazing thing about these OgoBild sticks and connectors is that he played and built alone for a long time.  This is a testament, I think, to the relative ease of building neat things with them.  The sticks are light and easy to manipulate, and the connector balls are pretty ingenious: flexible but firm, and easy for kids--even 4 year olds--to manipulate.  What is also neat is that these are big enough to build (small) structures to climb under and to cover with blankets.  In all, I would say that this is a really neat, very unique toy that was a hit with my child.As for important negatives:-I wish it came with a simple pull-string bag to store the pieces--the box will not hold up as a long terms storage solution, and because they are so long, we don't have a bag that will fit them.-I wish it came with a few more pieces--especially balls.  I figure with 2 sets you could pretty much go to town.That said, it's a neat toy and very good for learning to build things independently... and, perhaps as an added bonus, it has built-in geometric lessons which are applicable to electron shell orbital theory for future scientists!

reviewText: This is an interesting version of monopoly... first some quick facts or details worth knowing:1) Even though there are 6 tokens the game only accommodates 4 people because there are only 4 towers.2) The games really are short.  We played twice, once for 20 minutes and once for 25.3) The game has only 9 spaces per side.  We found this pretty disconcerting if you are used to monopoly versions with 10.Overall this game is fun.  The concept is interesting.  I'm not going to spend a lot of time talking about the premise as I'm going to assume that the Amazon description and other reviewers have thoroughly covered this.  Instead, I'll review.I like the game a lot..  that said, I would like it much better if it wasn't brand heavy with a lot of brands I dislike.  Featured brands (tokens) are Coke, Ducati (what?), Xbox, Chevrolet, McDonalds and Paramount.  I would do without the junk food for sure.  Another featured brand is Nestle, which is pretty much evil.  I don't like giving these companies product placement in my home.  Also, because of the brands, which include technology brands like spotify, beats by Dr. Dre and Samsung Mobile this game has a shelf life of a handful of years.  Honestly, because of the brand heavy emphasis, I'm not super eager to pull this out with my kids since testing it out.As far as play, my 10 year old found it easy to learn.  It has the regular benefit of money counting for kids, but that's about it.  Maybe some strategy in billboard swapping, but it's not exactly brain surgery.We found a couple issues with the instructions that could stand to be worked out in future releases -1) It is not clear if you are supposed to collect the amount UNDER the value of your highest billboard, or the value ABOVE the highest billboard.  We chose above.2) There is a little paradox with free parking that my 10 year old caught and proposed.  On free parking, you can either do nothing, or you can pay the bank $100K and move to any space on the board, collecting the value of your tower if you pass go and then play on that space.  There is nothing in the instructions that says you can't move to free parking again and do this as long as you want collecting money each time.  She proposed it and we vetoed.  Adding the word to any *other* space on the board in the instructions would be smart.3) It would be a nice variation to have a little more money to start.I think that's it.  Overall, I like it, but the brands are a big turnoff.

I don't like giving these companies product placement in my home. Honestly, because of the brand heavy emphasis, I'm not super eager to pull this out with my kids since testing it out.As far as play, my 10 year old found it easy to learn. It has the regular benefit of money counting for kids, but that's about it. Maybe some strategy in billboard swapping, but it's not exactly brain surgery.We found a couple issues with the instructions that could stand to be worked out in future releases -1) It is not clear if you are supposed to collect the amount UNDER the value of your highest billboard, or the value ABOVE the highest billboard. We chose above.2) There is a little paradox with free parking that my 10 year old caught and proposed. On free parking, you can either do nothing, or you can pay the bank $100K and move to any space on the board, collecting the value of your tower if you pass go and then play on that space. There is nothing in the instructions that says you can't move to free parking again and do this as long as you want collecting money each time. She proposed it and we vetoed. Adding the word to any *other* space on the board in the instructions would be smart.3) It would be a nice variation to have a little more money to start.I think that's it. reviewText: The premise is simple and very kid friendly. Add pouch #1 to bath water (very little bath water) and the water magically changes to blue goo. Play for a bit and then add pouch #2 to the tub and the goo will magically liquify.My daughter did take great delight with the science experiment aspect of it. So, we had to find out what it is: sodium polyacrylate (think disposable diaper granules). How it dissolves (salt, literally table salt) - so if you are having trouble dissolving it - just add more salt (e.g. table salt, and your problems will disappear, literally).However, it did not stand the fun test. One packet was not enough for even goobifying one 2.5 inch tub of water (standard tub, and yes, we got the ruler out). It was definitely not solid - a very loose gel, which is not particularly entertaining. So she lost interest in the goo itself in less than 10 minutes. Same thing second time. So, in the bath? Under our use, it was just a waste of bath water. If I were to use this again (highly doubtful I'd buy it), I would go for a sink or play tub - a much smaller container for better goo production. I'm not thrilled about putting it down the sink either, so a plastic tub would help avoid that. Realistically, I'd milk the science experiment aspect and just make my own -Superabsorbent Diaper Polymer 1 lb Sodium Polyacrylate.Bottom line: Meh. Not worth it.

reviewText: This is a fairly simple game where one selects square cards that have one or more of three paths: train tracks, road, or river. The game is a bit like dominos, where a single card is used to begin play and then turns procede with each player trying to continue the paths. For example, if the first card has tracks and road, the next card down needs to have tracks and a road. On some cards, one path ends and/or another begins, so it changes as you go. You start with 10 cards in your hand and pick one each turn from a much larger number. The object is to get rid of all your cards.My two six year old boys (who love cars, boats, and trains) and I played this game. The problem is that, more often than not, there wasn't a card in their pile of 10+ cards that matched either of the two ends. We'd go turn after turn not being able to make the game any larger. This was very frustrating and not at all fun. The number of cards in our hands just increased and eventually we gave up.There seemed to be too many cards overall. There seemed to be not enough chance that you'll use a card. And there seemed to be a lack of strategy. There are cards that allow branching, where one path goes straight and another turns, so the path bifurcates. But this didn't happen often so we played mostly with just two ends.I would like to try it again, but this time start with four corner cards plased so that there are 8 active paths. I think that would be a lot more fun for the boys and make this tolerable. However my boys don't want to play this again, so I'll have to do some convincing.The cards are well made, colorful, and nicely drawn. Clearly some thought went into its production; too bad the game play wasn't better thought through.

reviewText: The Fisher-Price Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table is a nice addition for those little chefs who want to do some pretend-play in their kitchen, but it also friendly to families who are hard-up for space (like we are). Basically the Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table does double duty as both a kitchen, and as a standard table, and does a good job at both.Assembly was quick and fairly easy, taking roughly half an hour to go from a pile of plastic pieces (14) and screws (24) to the completed product. The table seems very sturdy once completed and is a good height for my toddler at the higher setting (with the "oven" attached; the lower setting seems practically useless).In "kitchen mode," the stovetop basically makes three sounds, bubbling, boiling on the burner, sizzling on the grill and the ticking and "ding" of the oven timer (along with a red light in the oven itself). It's simple, but it works, and my daughter likes turning the knobs while she pretends to cook. Turn the stovetop over, and you have a flat table-top and then the Servin' Surprises table looks very much like any other toddler/play-table out there. You can take the oven off as well, but we just leave it there, as I would imagine most would.Another plus with the Servin' Surprises table is that it comes with a lot of accessories: the "Magical" serving tray, cookies to bake (with cookie sheet), a pizza that can go from veggie to pepperoni and plates, cups, forks, etc. ("service for two," as the description calls it). Fisher-Price also makes Servin' Surprises add-on items for the Servin' Surprises Kitchen, so you can expand that a good bit (my daughter will be getting the Tea Party Set for Christmas). I like the fact that you can life the center piece off to reveal a storage compartment for the accessories.Overall, we've been very satisfied with this table, but there are a couple of things that stop it from being flawless. The oven door is difficult to open and close, just about requiring an adult to do it (and even then, it takes some fiddling to get it to close properly). The door of the oven has no "glass," so it's just an open hole, which was a bit disappointing, and the pizza pan very barely fits in the oven. The table also doesn't come with chairs (and doesn't claim to), but it would be nice if Fisher Price offered some that were made for it. The lack of batteries (requires 6AA batteries between the stovetop and serving tray) isn't surprising to me (seems like nothing comes with batteries these days), but it would have been nice had they been included. Remember to buy some...Those things are minor quibbles, and all-in-all, the Fisher Price Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table is a great addition. reviewText: I have a bias about board games compared to video games...they just seem to encourage interaction rather than isolation. So I'm always on the look-out for a new game that everyone can enjoy. When this came up the description and other reviews were very encouraging so I decided to give it a try.Essentially it is a great game espcially if you have kids of different ages and/or abilities. I also appreciate the fact it stimulates memory and attention span without putting younger children at an immense disadvantage like spelling, strategy or other types of games. However, very young children wouldn't be able to keep up - hence the instructions that it is fun for kids 8 and up - including adults.The last statement is the disappointment. While this is a fun game for adults to play with kids, it wouldn't be much fun for just adults...at least none of the adults I know. It's simply far too silly for older teens or adults without the benefit of young kids.So - great game for...Grandparents, aunts and uncles that may want to interact with kids when visiting.Teachers or baby-sitters who want something different that still encourages kids to pay attention but have fun.Parents with elementary aged kids or families with a range of ages.Not so great game for...Adult only households.Teens.Update: I'd like to add that after playing this with a few kids and adult get-togethers it quickly became the kids absolute favorite! They were begging to play again (and again) until the adults just couldn't take it. The more absurd the better and they just thrilled and delighted in watching uptight adults act like a monkey or some such craziness. However, there is an educational aspect and it does increase attention span while encouraging memorization and creativity. If you have kids around the age of ten this might actually become a new favorite!
summary: Great Family Fun if you have kids

reviewText: Thomas & Friends have long been a friend for toddlers, who enjoy watching the antics on TV and playing with their Thomas toys at home. Now a new choice that promotes creative thinking and dexterity as well as play is available in the Thomas & Friends - Sodor Friends floor puzzle.The 24-piece, 3 x 2 feet shaped floor puzzle for ages 3 and older is made by Ravensburger, founded in 1891 and in 2012 acclaimed as the world's greatest puzzle brand. Ravensburger puzzle pieces are made durable enough to withstand the demands of little hands and promote the development of fine motor skills, association, task completion and independent play.The European company, a leading supplier of puzzles and games around the world, has 8,000 different products - 85 percent of which they make themselves. The German-based company employs more than 1,400 workers.The hand-cutting tools used by Ravensburger to make Thomas & Friends - Sodor Friends are such that no two pieces are alike. The pieces fit together easily to reveal seven brightly-colored trains and are strong enough that they don't break. Made from recycled boards, the grained paper provides a glare-free picture.Your kids don't really have to be Thomas fans to enjoy this wonderful puzzle.

reviewText: "Don't Make Me Laugh" is an improvisation game - akin to charades but with talking/sound effects and much more interactivity.  There is "solo" play when one acts out a scene alone, partner play where the player chooses a partner to act out the scene together, and all-play mode when everyone BUT the player gets in on the action.  If you've got a group of players who are able to let their hair down (even a little bit), good luck not laughing!Each player is handed a card and has to act out the situation.  (There are no off-color or suggestive cards - everything is appropriate for kids.)  The parnter and group-play cards are where the fun really begins.  Some favorites that got the biggest guffaws include, "You are a cowboy trying to get an wandering cow back in its pen", "You've just spotted a huge bug in a friend's hair", "You're playing dodgeball.  Try not to get hit", "You're in a marching band marching in the wrong direction", and "Make up a quick cheer!"  (That last one displayed two dads baring belly buttons, finishing with a two-man pyramid.  Awesome.)A brilliant twist on this game are the "Awards" cards.  You'll not just vote for your favorite, you'll vote for "Bravest Performance", "Most Dramatic Performance", "Most Impressive Performance", "Most Energetic Performance", etc...  This opens the door for younger players who may not have great dramatic chops but can sure bounce like a super ball to score big.  If you don't think you can get "Most Thoughtful Performance", you can shoot for "Most Energetic".This game's inherent flexibility is both a blessing (because you can easily modify it to fit your group's needs) and a curse (because if following the rules verbatim is somewhat confusing).  The game states right in the instructions, if you don't like these instructions, make up your own!  I can almost guarantee you'll do this and enjoy the experience for it.  Our modifications including jettisoning the entire scoring system for merely pointing at the person/team that best fits the award.  Most of the props that come with the game (a clown nose, inflexible - and therefore difficult to use - wrist bands, scoring cups) are completely unnecessary to play the game well and have a great time.  The cards (and willingness to put yourself "out there") are king.So, the instructions are a bit confusing and the kit comes with stuff you won't use... This is STILL a 5-star game based on the fun-factor alone.  Highly recommended for good, clean fun at family reunions, church functions, youth groups, city counsel meetings, group therapy, funerals, and office parties.  Not recommended for the orchestra or doctor's office, solely because of spontaneous outbursts of laughter.

reviewText: Overall the table is great for those babies just starting to stand and 'walk' while holding onto furniture and others things.Good:- Lots of buttons to push- Super easy "assembly"- Counts numbers (1-10) and sings the ABC. And does some basic colors.- Interactions are all different and require the baby to think about how to interact with each element. Some are for spinning, others pushing, flipping, pulling. Some noises are mechanical, others are electronic/sounds.- Lights (our baby tries to eat those light int he center of the table)Neutral:- very light weight. Which is both good and bad. Good because if it fall on your toddler's feet of tummy, it won't really do any damage. Bad because it's easy for the baby to pull it to the floor.- Not really sure what baby is learning, but she likes banging on the table, and seems to like the numbers song quite a bit.- Very small (easy to store, fits anywhere, but I expected it to be a little larger) It's just a little smaller than a regular office chair.Cons:- Easy to topple over. Baby cannot hold onto it and pull themselves up. (Or they can, if you hold the table so it doesn't tip over)- Legs have no rubber at the bottom or anything to keep them from slidingOverall this is a fun toy that provides a small area where babies can walk while holding onto something. It slips very easily on the floor, and baby would be unable to stand up by themselves. However, it is more stable in carpet so with a little help baby can start standing up without your assistance.

reviewText: Clad in his Mark 42 armor and equipped with a missile firing arm and various electronic sounds and phrases, the Iron Man 3 Sonic Blasting Action Figure is ready for battle! For whatever reason (to cut down on packaging maybe), the figure's legs are cut off just below the knees. The feet are in the box, but you have to assemble them. Once that's done, Iron Man stands a good 14 inches and looks pretty impressive.The good - the press-button firing is pretty darned cool. That barrel just spins and fires until it's empty, and you get some cool sound effects while it is going. The figure is also very detailed and makes a neat shelf piece.The not so good - to accommodate the firing mechanism and electronics, there is very little articulation with this figure. It's kind of lame as action figures go. They also give you twice as many missiles as the figure can hold, which is fine, but nowhere to store the extras. A couple of clips on the back or arms would have solved this. Instead those extras are bound to be lost.This is a big, hefty toy with some very cool features. It's probably not idea for smaller kids looking for an action figure to take with them, but older kids ought to get a kick out of the Iron Man 3 Sonic Blasting Action Figure.

reviewText: In a world where everything's gotta be so freaking digital, it was nice to be able to sit down for a quiet evening, soft music playing in the background, and work on a jigsaw puzzle -- old-school style.I must have been in a very nostalgic mood when I sat down to work on this puzzle, because I noticed everything. The box itself is well-constructed, none of that dry, rough thin cardboard stuff you find at the dollar store. It's smooth and glossy, and sturdy. The puzzle pieces inside felt the same way, and came contained in a clear plastic bag. I tore it open and got down to business.The box says the 300-piece puzzle is appropriate for ages 8 and up. And the puzzle pieces are about 1" x 1", up to 1" x 2" and even 1" x 3" -- so the pieces are easy for adults and kids to handle. I didn't have to squint and figure out what the heck I was looking at (horror stories from those 1000 to 2000 piece monstrosities!). But there's a very appropriate level of difficulty as well. Several pieces are cut in a varied, entertaining way (which adds a surprisingly higher level of difficulty at times) -- but the curves and notches are distinct. You'll get that giddy feeling when finding interlocking pieces, and they all fit perfectly -- as they should!The puzzle, the box says, should be 18" x 24" -- so I was able to work on it on our $20 Ikea coffee table without too much inconvenience. If I had begun on a larger surface, I think I would have had an easier time. No time wasted negotiating precious real estate. But that's my fault for not planning ahead!There were 300 pieces -- each and every last whimsical one accounted for -- and the picture on the box clearly showed me what I was aiming for. No repeating themes or patterns, which was very nice.It really has been a while since I've done a puzzle, so this was a nice one to pick up. You'll find fun pieces (electric guitar, boot, people shapes, helicopter, thumbs up, and others -- yeah, this ain't your grandma's puzzle!). It was fun to sort out the pieces, find the edges, and all that.I had a lot of fun, and it was nice to enjoy a quiet evening, gathered around the living room coffee table with the TV off. It took me 4 hours to finish this puzzle by myself, but I wouldn't mind doing it again!

I like that you can use a separate brush for each color to prevent accidental color mixing.The brushes are very large, so they work well with an easel.  The handles are rounded and easy for a young child to grip.  The handles are also entirely made of plastic, including the part that looks like metal.  I usually prefer wood, but the plastic makes clean-up very easy.  I can just soak the brushes in a cup of water without worrying about rust or damaged wood.If you need paint brushes to use on smaller sheets of paper, I'd recommend ones that are smaller than these.  For big paintings, though, they are wonderful!
summary: Great paint brushes for young children!

reviewText: Yuck! This stuff makes an unimaginable mess. First of all to achieve the level of goo as described in the instructions by gradually adding water is does not take into consideration the users of the product - children. My grandkids, 10-year old girl and 3-year old boy, dumped both pouches in the tub and kept adding water, lots of and lots of water. The result was a bathtub full of gelatin marbles, which stuck to everything and I do mean everything - kids, floors, fixtures, pets, walls, towels, rugs, carpet. The 10-year old was grossed out. The 3-year old said it felt like a wet diaper - and he would know.If this slime is "environmentally safe" I'm a monkey's uncle. The dissolve solution doesn't work. The bathtub drain clogged. I used 2 pounds of dead sea salt and still had to scoop out about 2 quarts of goo and use drain cleaner.I notice that some people recommend using this stuff outside. But why would you even want this crap on your kids' skin? Or risk your pets getting into it. Or getting it on your grass. I can't imagine how you would dispose of it. And I can't possibly recommend this stuff - unless your idea of fun is making a huge mess and spending the rest of the day cleaning it up. I think they should take this stuff off the market.

reviewText: My daughter (5) is quite the tea party buff. She has even been able to convince her two brothers to join her for tea parties and has thrown "official" tea parties for her friends. She was my official tester for this set. This set definitely has the cuteness factor you would expect in a tea set. It also food grade, meaning you can put drinks (like lemonade) in the cups, food on the plates, etc. This is important because some manufacturers are stupid enough to put tea sets on the market using materials that aren't food grade - so kids can't really use them!The set worked well. Don't overfill the teapot or it can leak, but this is still good for a "party".These are NOT dishwasher safe. Not a bad thing since clean up is a fun and important part of any tea party anyway (and washing dishes instead of just throwing them in the dishwasher should happen sometimes). They also should NOT have hot liquids or be placed in the microwave. Now, this isn't a bad thing since this set is recommended for kids as young as 3 and I can't see serving a 3 year old tea with boiling water.We didn't quite get the "sunny patch" design. It has cute butterfly designs and the teapot is kind of a flower, but for "Sunny Patch" we were thinking Mrs. Spider's Sunny Patch so we were kind of thrown off by that.Overall a really good tea set that a child can actually use (no BPA or PVC - THANK YOU!!!). Just be careful with it (no microwave, no dishwasher) and it should last a long time!

reviewText: First, the toy came with no instructions, but with a little bit of work, I was able to put the Ipad into the art frame.  Then with a puzzled look, I tried to figure out how the frame actually interacted with the Ipad.  Let me make this easy for anyone interested in this, you need to load the free App into the Ipad to use the accessories (including stamps and crayon-like stylist).So, here is my recommendation for anyone interested in this product.  First, download the free app (no ads, which makes it extra desirable), and then decide if your child likes the app enough to start buying the accessories.  But you should also consider if the frame is even needed for your child.  If you've got a protective holder that tilts, you might be happy with just that, but if that doesn't tilt or seems suspect, you might consider getting the frame that is essentially this product.  I'm also a bit suspicious that the frame is not going to protect the Ipad from a drop.  It is made of plastic with a snap lock.  But I'm certainly not going to do any drop tests to find out!  The shapes and crayon have some value, but I'd say the most value has to do with the size for little hands.As far as the free app goes, I do like that and think that it does foster creative play.  The frame itself seems overpriced for what you get (everything is plastic), but if you think that it suits the need of your child as outlined earlier, it is well worth the price to get them doing something other than playing mindless games on some app that has an ad every 30 seconds.  I should add that my child is five and has no trouble at all navigating through the app, but he is one of those kids who has been Ipad proficient since the age of 2 (probably as are most children).
summary: Nice art app, but what you're buying is the Ipad holder and stamps

reviewText: I ordered this, well, because it looked cool. And then I got it and read the instructions, and my heart sank a little. It seemed minimally interactive. And then I plugged it in and my heart sunk a little more -- "cool" talking instructions accompanied by spacey sound effects. But we dutifully put in a wax stick, put in a mold (you have your choice of truck or sports car), pushed a button, and waited. However-many-minutes later, we pulled out the mold to see a warm, waxy mess. Let's just say the future of this toy was looking grim at that point. So why the four stars? Because we've gone on to successfully make nine other molds (and one other complete dud) and we still have FOUR sticks of wax left.Because the cars don't require an entire stick of wax to make, some of the cars end up being a fusion of color. A good-looking fusion, that's different each time. As far as I can tell, you have no control over whether or not that fusion will happen (and because of the way you have to preload the wax sticks, you may not even have a good idea of what color car you're going to end up with), but we've ended up with some beautiful models.Most of the car-"making" process is easy enough for my daughter to do. The one thing I insist on an adult doing is removing the car from the mold -- a somewhat tricky, somewhat time-consuming process. Everything else -- inserting the wax and the mold, pressing the button and lever, removing the mold and excess wax, and customizing the wax car with the included stickers -- is straightforward enough.All the sights and sounds are kind of gimmicky and the machine is a little too automated for my taste, but the process still manages to be somewhat cool. I am skeptical about how scratch- and heat-resistant these little wax cars might be, and I wish the kit came with more chassis, but it's still a fun product. This would be neat for a family with a lot of Hot Wheel lovers or, if you bought extra chassis, as novelty gifts for visitors. In my situation, with one child, the toy seems a bit extravagant (how many wax car tops does one kid need? and yes, we've given some away to guests), and I'm skeptical about how many people will find it worth the price. Despite all these caveats, everyone in my family *likes* it so it gets the "I like it" number of stars. Is it for you and your family? Well, at least now you know more so you can decide.

reviewText: The Scotch gift wrap cutter is very good at two tasks. The first is cutting wrapping paper. In my tests it proved easier to use than my legacy methods of really sharp scissors and the two step method of making a fold at the cut point and then using a carving knife to make the cut. With the GWC, all you have to do is find the spot you want to cut the paper from the roll, slip the bottom lip of the cutter underneath the paper and then push it straight across the roll. I found that I could cut a reasonably straight line by just using the roll as a guide. It was fast and easy.The next task was to cut and curl ribbon. I used both a PVC sparkly plastic ribbon and standard curling ribbon while wrapping two packages. The cutter can also cut ribbon to length, and it worked fine for this. Then, I tied some extra strands of ribbon to the top of each of the two test packages as a bow and curled the ends. The ribbon curling feature worked just fine, although I felt that it took a couple tries to get my technique down to the point that the curls were as tight as those using scissors.Overall, no complaints. This is the "go to" tool for package wrapping.
