reviewText: As did other Vine members, I received a huge box from Mattel, that included many other components in addition to this track builder starter set. The simple track builder starter set is what I'm required to review, so I'm trying to limit the majority of my comments here to that starter unit, though I may not succeed in doing that.My five year old grandson loves cars, and he played with the entire "set" (beyond just this track starter set) for six hours straight and he loves most of the components, including this starter set.  His mother did find one complaint, namely that the base of the tower has track extensions that aren't really useful, because they run into the tracks above, when connected. In her opinion, elbow turns would make a great launcher option, as the elbow connectors would eliminate this problem. Also, my grandkids were a little frustrated because the tracks "just end", and so the cars would wind up under couches, etc.  This reminds me that these units don't function nearly as well on carpet as they do on hard floors, or even sidewalks!As other reviewers have said, a few of the components in the entire set that Vine members received, have some peculiarities and do not function quite as well as certain other units do, but overall I would say that most young kids between 4 or 5 and up to at least age 9, would very much like this starter set, and many of the other components. My 8 year old granddaughter loved playing with the whole set, until her 5 year old brother (and his friends) ran her off....on the other hand, she was the creative one who thought to set the entire configuration up outside on the sidewalk, which of course drew half the neighborhood over to see the excitement...I highly recommend that any potential buyer (of either this starter set or of other component add-ons) read all of the Amazon reviews for the individual units or components that they want to buy, and make your buying choices based on the reviews. Oh, and one other nice thing about the whole set that I received:  the kids seemed to love being creative and moving around tracks and units, etc. They were fascinated with their own creativity, LOL.

reviewText: My son is a bit too young to play with the Matchbox Mission: Croc Escape Playset so I took the opportunity to try this toy out with my 9yr old nephew recently and gauge his reaction and fun with the toy. The playset is designed for children 3-10.The very first thing you have to know is that adult assembly is required. Though my nephew was able to help me out it still took a solid 10-15 minutes to get the set assembled. My first impression wasn't great - the track is rather large and cumbersome and seemingly not very well made. The highlight is definitely the die-cast off-road truck that comes with the set. But this set only includes one vehicle. The other major detraction is that the toy doesn't break down easily for storage. My son's closet includes several large deep drawers that we use to store toys. This playset is entirely too large for those and has to be stored in his room on the floor.For its size the set has limited fun potential. There is a car elevator to ascend a set of jungle stairs, the ramp with a few obstacles/traps and then the crocodile jaws which can clamp shut and trap the die-cast truck. That's it. For the price of the set I understand that there are limitations but by itself this toy is extremely limited in its entertainment value. There are additional tracks and cars that can be purchased and build on each other but at added expense.For my nephew this was an interesting diversion for about 10 minutes before he wanted to do something else. My advice is to pass on this toy unless you're looking to build out a large set with multiple vehicles.

reviewText: These Leappad products are definitely kid proof. This model has replaceable and rechargeable batteries which is nice. The Ultra version batteries are not user replaceable which is a big downside of that model. Battery life is good, I'd guess about 10 hours or so. Our son uses them on long car trips without them losing power.We have two Leap Pads. One is this LeapPad2 model and the other is the Ultra (free to us as Vine members). As far as the product itself they are fine and the biggest advantage of them is they are very sturdy and kid proof. Our 4-year-old son has put them both through the test, hitting the screen very hard with the stylus, getting the screen wet and putting his food covered fingers on the screen. They clean up and perform perfectly.The apps are mostly pretty good, one big advantage is they are voice directed so if the little on can't read they still can use the apps. I must say our 4-year-old learned the alphabet by himself with the LeapPad in about a week.The really big downside, and the one that makes me mark it two stars, is the apps are way too expensive. Some can be had for about $5 but they are far from the best apps. Many of them are $25. Yes you can often find sales but that takes 10-20% off the price reducing the $25 apps down to perhaps $20 - still very expensive.In an era when you can buy a 7" tablet (not kid proof) for under $100 and load it up with good apps which are anywhere from free to $5 I just can't see spending the outrageous prices for the leap apps. I'm guessing it is a matter of volume. If LeapFrog sold in huge volume like tablet apps do then the prices might come down.Purchase a dozen apps for the LeapPad and you've likely spent upwards of $200.We have purchased a few apps for the LeapPad but tend to buy way less expensive apps for our smartphones and let our son play with them. The LeapPad is used less and less now. We will likely buy our son a 7" tablet next.
summary: Nice but apps are very expensive

reviewText: My 2-year-old has a lot of play food and related items for her play kitchen including theGreen Toys Dish Setwhich is one of the highest quality playsets I've ever seen. It set the bar for us regarding play food/dishes and made our other sets (painted wood) look really pathetic. I've even tossed them on the top rack of my dishwasher when daddy decided to give her soda in the tea cups. [insert motherly facepalming here]All that to say that if you're going to buy toys that can hold up to some serious beatings look no further than Green Toys. We chose this set because it's so different from anything out there. It's a clever/sneaky way to encourage healthy eating through play. The vinager, olive oil, salt, and pepper items are all light cardboard and require folding to put together which is a little confusing. They didn't hold up well either, which is why I only rated the durability a 3 (otherwise it'd get a 5). Within 3 days the pepper was completely ripped apart and the vinegar had been crushed a few times requiring popping back into tabs and such. Otherwise the plastic parts have all survived just fine. If you're giving these to a younger kid like mine you may want to tuck those away for adult supervised playtime so they don't suffer the roughness of a toddler.As a bit of an aside we've actually come up with an additional game to play with the veggies/fruits. My little one loves math and is learning counting so we've been practicing first counting how many of each item there are, then counting how many 'greens', 'reds', and 'whites' there are, and then laying them out to form patterns (ie. lettuce, cucumbers, tomato, lettuce, cucumbers, 'now what comes next?'). There aren't too many to confuse her and she's learning as we play.TheGreen Toys 16 Piece Salad Setis well made, Earth-friendly (visit the Green Toys website to learn all about it), made in the U.S.A., and is so attractive. A definite recommendation from us if you want a great play set for your play kitchen.

reviewText: A few of my son's friends had this game, so when his 4th birthday rolled around and he had some money to spend, we decided to get it for our house.  We love it!The object of the game is so simple-- you catch the lightweight butterflies that fly out of the elephant's trunk in a net.  Then you count the butterflies, and whoever has the most wins.  We don't usually compete, though-- it's fun enough just to watch my kids run around and attempt to catch the butterflies.  My one and a half year old just picks them off the floor, but she still has so much fun with it.  It's one of the only games that we can play together where she can participate.  And although it's not extremely educational, you do count the butterflies at the end, and it does take coordination to catch the butterflies.I suppose some of the "flaws" are true-- the elephant has to be on a flat surface to work.  It works for us on our carpeted floor, but I can also place a hardback book under the elephant to make sure the fan goes.  All the butterflies don't usually fly out, but my kids don't seem to care if there's a handful left when we go to play it again.  And it does involve parent participation-- I need to make sure the nose is completely straight and the opening on the top is open in order for the butterflies to fly out.  But I don't mind, even if I have to do that every couple minutes.  The main flaw I see is that our nose is starting to get bent and I wouldn't be surprised if it tears one day, but I'm sure if that happens, we'll have gotten plenty of use out of the game first.  :)Anyway, highly recommended.

reviewText: This toy does a good job of what it claims to do: it asks a series of questions, you answer with any of a few scripted answers (yes, no, it depends, i don't know), and it deduces what animal you're thinking of. Maybe i just lack imagination, but i haven't been able to come up with an animal it can't figure out (though Tyrannosaurus did take a while). It has some personality, with a few witty comments mixed in with the questions about the animals size, color, and so on.It has some trouble in noisy environments, which isn't a surprise.In all, though, after a few rounds of 20 questions, the toy just isn't that fun anymore. It's one of those things that will completely absorb a child's attention for 5-15 minutes, then they never touch it again. Maybe if it did more than just animals, it would be more fun, but maybe not. I think it's a lot better suited to have out at parties, where kids can take turns and make it a social thing, or maybe at a school where it could be used as anything from simple entertainment to an example of deductive reasoning.

reviewText: There are 5 major train sets for 3 to 5 year olds: (1) Vario (also known as Thomas and Friends Wooden Railway), (2) Thomas and Friends Take-n-Play, (3) Thomas and Friends Trackmaster, (4) LEGO Duplo Trains, and (5) Chuggington.Vario is by far the perennial favorite, with makers ranging from Thomas and Friends Wooden Railway, BRIO, PlanToys, Melissa & Doug, IKEA, and many others. Unfortunately, Chuggington chose to go proprietary route, which is rather unfortunate as the series have some truly excellent tracks and buildings while their die-cast trains leave much to be desired.Chugginton Die-Cast Wilson's Wild Ride is a prime example. The set consists of several dozen plastic tracks and bridge supports that snap together to build many different layouts (the manual provides instructions for building 1 layout as well as 3 finished layouts that most adults should be able to reconstruct easily).While plastic isn't highest of quality (much closer to Trackmaster than Duplo), the tracks are very durable and snaps with a satisfying click. My 3-year old son was able to put the tracks together with minimal help. The set includes a train yard that releases the train with electric sound effects and manual release lever, construction cones (where cones pop out when the train passes by), and turntable (which rotates several times as the train passes by).The default layout is quite entertaining, especially if your child is into roller coasters as mine is. My son was eager to build 3 alternate layouts, which took about 5 minutes to build.Included is Wilson (die-cast) and a cargo hopper car (plastic). Compared to Thomas, the train feels rather flimsy.My child has a ton of Vario tracks and trains (Thomas, PlanToys) and he was very disappointed to learn that he couldn't' combine them to build larger layout (they are just subtly different enough to be not compatible).
summary: Lots of fun but not Thomas compatible

reviewText: The Hot Wheels Workshop Track Builder Starter Set is a great center piece for any Hot Wheels set-up as you can have five cars start from the central tower.One aspect about the "Starter Set" is that it is a starter set, and you need to purchase some other Hot Wheels Builder Stunts and accessories to get full enjoyment of the set-up.  This is probably why Mattel sent with the Starter Set a number of Builder Stunt set-ups for me to try.  Of the ones they included in addition to the TRack Builder Starter Set,  theHot Wheels Track Builder Deluxe Quick Kick Loop Stunt SetandHot Wheels Track Builder Crossroad Crash Stunt Packseemed to generate the most excitement when added to this set-up.  So, plan on spending around $50-60 more if you don't already have some Hot Wheels cars and accessories.  BTW, one reviewer mentioned there were 5 cars included in his set. The track is easy to set-up, but it is far more difficult to break-down, but this is good, because you don't have to worry about it coming apart like these tracks did when I was growing-up.  Be sure to allow your youngsters additional time to put these tracks away.  You should, also, have an 8 gallon plastic container to store the pieces because there is no way you will be able to get all the pieces back into the box after taking them out.Overall, it's a great set and reasonably priced for what you get.

reviewText: I was a bit skeptical about this puzzle, namely how sturdy it was going to be, and how easily the structure would hold its shape.  That said, the Puzzleball was fun to put together, and holds up really well.  The pieces are hard plastic, and generally fit quite well with each other.  The ball holds its shape nicely while you build it, although putting the last pieces in (the north or south pole, depending on how you started) is a bit trickier, since you can only push from the inside.  You can build it two ways.  The easier way is by using the numbers on the back of each piece, and the harder way is by visually fitting the pieces, like any normal puzzle.  Due to the 3D nature and abundance of blue pieces, this second method is more of a challenge, especially for younger puzzlers. Recommended.

reviewText: I wanted something to really nail down the letter sounds for my eager to learn toddler.  Having had some experience with other Leap Frog Alphabet toys (I was a nanny for a while, and worked in daycares for even longer) I knew what I was ordering.  I was really happy to see that it was available with the storage for the letters, as they always seemed to be scattered everywhere.  A few things that I have noticed about this ...1 - The letters are a bit ... lighter and not as substantial as the older Leap Frog alphabet sets I've had experience with.  They are, by far not chinsy or cheap, they are sturdy ... just lighter than I remember them being.  Because of this, I don't know if they would be compatible with the older sets ... just a thought.2 -  The lid makes it a bit top heavy ... not a HUGE problem but .....3 - The lid doesn't really lock on well.  This is a positive, and a negative.  I like that my daughter can easily get them out whenever she wants to and I'm not having to help her open them up.  However, I wish it did lock in a bit better to prevent the lid from popping off and letters scattering everywhere at the slightest bump.4 - The base stores the letters ... which is AWESOME!  But there isn't a GPS installed in the letters to find them when they do scatter,wish there was some sort of magnetic clean up button to draw them in, because as an anal retentive mother, I am always dumping them out every night to make sure that A - Z are all there ... they usually aren't.  The letters like to hide under the couch, in case you end up with missing letters -- check there first.Overall, it is a great buy, and I'm thrilled to have it in the house.  My toddler loves it.  I love it.  My hubs loves it.  And any future siblings are going to love it.  :)

reviewText: We're not tournament players, more like casual players and I thought with this new electronic banking, it would speed things up a bit. My first impressions of the game were: "Whoa, they changed a lot!" and they did. All the money amounts are upgraded. For example, every time you pass Go your salary is now 2 Million. Yes, MILLION. But of course this is not dollars, they have changed the currency so all the dollar signs are replaced with a Monopoly currency symbol which is an M with a line through it. The Community Chest and Chance have all been modernized as well. Gone is the winning the beauty pageant, instead you win the lottery. You get put in jail for identity theft. They also changed the little token pieces too. You now have a cell phone, a skateboard, an airplane, burger, race car and roller blade.Those things are more of less superficial and don't change the game play, but some of the changes were more significant. When you land on income tax, you don't get to choose the 10% or 2 Million, you have to forgo your entire salary. There is a card that sends you to the utilities but you pay less than what you would normally had to landed there on a dice roll. This was counter to the older game where you would pay more. This made the utilities less appealing to buy.As to the actual electronic banking aspect, we didn't like it. People knew how much money you had because the banker can see your total, and you had to keep checking with him to see what your balance is. With a transaction like "Pay each player 50" in the old way you would just hand them a single bill but here there's all this card swiping and messing with the machine. It didn't make our game any faster, nor any easier.
summary: A modernized version that is neither more fun or faster to play

As he improves, I intend to make my instructions more vague to force him to ask clarifying questions.  He also learned some new vocabulary words, like "structure" and "attributes."It's difficult to tell the scale from the photograph, but the blocks are much larger than I expected, large enough to be nice for my daughter with cerebral palsy to work on fine motor skills like stacking.  The cards are around twice as long as standard playing cards.

Making him be the instruction giver without being allowed to use his hands is also a good challenge. As he improves, I intend to make my instructions more vague to force him to ask clarifying questions. He also learned some new vocabulary words, like "structure" and "attributes."It's difficult to tell the scale from the photograph, but the blocks are much larger than I expected, large enough to be nice for my daughter with cerebral palsy to work on fine motor skills like stacking. The cards are around twice as long as standard playing cards.

reviewText: Before this arrived, but after ordering it, I read the reviews here and everyone was talking about how cheap and flimsy the construction was, how poorly it worked, etc., so needless to say I was a bit worried.But honestly there's nothing wrong with this set at all!The dome is relatively thin plastic, sure, but it's strong and rigid and not anything like a "plastic drink bottle" as I think one reviewer described it. If I hadn't read all the negative reviews I don't think it would have occurred to me to comment on the thickness of the plastic, as it's completely adequate for this application.As far as how well it works, it seems to be at least as good (probably better) than most of the "battle tops" stuff. Sure, there's a big chance that you drop both spinning tops into the dome and they mostly just go "plunk" and lay on the bottom spinning down. But every few tries you can actually get the two tops racing around the dome, and you can get some pretty good action from a single top which will orbit the inside of the dome for several seconds. Again, it doesn't work every time, and maybe works less than you would like, but it does work.Personally I don't really get the appeal of these top battle things though, and our 5yo did get bored with it relatively quickly. The whole concept seems kind of silly for the amount of marketing and product development they've put into it. The way that the tops work, they kind of hang from the launcher thing when it looks like they should attach securely, so the whole thing seems a lot less satisfying than it could be. But this is just my grown-up observation of the whole battle tops thing, and not a criticism of this set specifically.But this toy is fine for what it is.G.

I introduced it to my friends, explained the rules, and had a game, all within 30 minutes. I highly recommend it.

reviewText: We purchased both a Fisher Price Laugh and Learn Table and a LeapStart Learning Table.  The plan was to see which one our daughter (7 months at the time) liked best.  We would keep the one she liked best at home and send the other to Grandma and Grandpa's house.  Here is how the two compare.1.  The Fisher Price table is shorter than the LeapStart table and baby seems to be able to pull up on it at a younger age. Baby can also sit at the Fisher Price table easier because it is lower.2.  Both have stable legs and do not tip over when baby leans up against them or pushes on them. Both have legs that can be removed for floor play when baby can not stand.  (We never used it this way because our daughter was early to stand.)3.  Both have a learning mode with ABC song and counting to 10 song and a musical mode.4.  In the musical mode the Laugh and Learn table plays tunes to familiar children's songs.  It has a traditional feel to the music.  The LeapStart table has music based on the different instruments on the table such as a banjo tune, a sax sound, etc. and it has a jazzier feel to the music.5.  The Laugh and Learn table has a food theme and looks like a set table.  In the learning mode concepts such as color, shapes, texture, manners, shapes, open/shut, empty/full, peek-a-boo, and naming of common items such as apple, blueberries, banana, juice, etc.  The LeapStart table has a musical theme with instruments such as a piano, maracas, sax, violin, and banjo.  In the learning mode concepts include colors, shapes, high, low, on, off, hello, goodbye, etc.6.  On the Laugh and Learn table the parent has to change the mode.  On the LeapStart table the child can change the mode by turning the page on the book in the center of the table.7.  The Laugh and Learn table has a bowl in the center that spins and can hold favorite objects.  The LeapStart table has a small purple door that can hold favorite objects in the indentation underneath the door.As a parent, I like the LeapStart table more.  The music is parent friendly and even after repeated use, it does not annoy adults.  I also like the different musical instruments and musical sounds that are introduced.  That said, my daughter (now 9 months) likes the Laugh and Learn table better.  She likes putting objects like small balls, Cheerios, and her pacifier in the bowl in the center.  She also likes the peek-a-boo napkin with the peas underneath which says "Peek-a-boo.  I see you." when she opens the door.  It makes her laugh. Another favorite is the spoon rattle that can be removed from the table and the alphabet letters that float in the water sealed in the bowl that move around when the bowl spins.  This is her favorite toy.  She does play with the LeapStart table at her Grandparents house now, but her attention span is short with this toy.  She can play with her Laugh and Learn table for long periods of time.

reviewText: I got this game for my grandkids, ages 5 and 7. This is a really easy game to learn and it is quick, so even children with short attention spans will be able to finish the game. All the children need to be able to recognize is color. You line up the wooden snails and roll both dice, whatever color shows up on the dice gets to move forward one space. The snail to reach the finish line first is the winner. It is that simple. We had a lot of fun playing with the kids, and they were able to play together without help once they had played a couple of games. I even found one of the kids playing by himself and racing all of the snails just to see which one would win. It is a quick, quiet game that will keep your children busy for a while. We even varied the game by only using one dice, which made the game a little longer. We also chose a color of a snail not being used and made up a rule that if anyone rolled that color, their snail went back a space. The possibilities are only limited by your imagination. I highly recommend this game.

reviewText: Timeline: Inventions is one of many sets of cards in the Timeline series.The game pits player's temporal cognizance against each other to lay down inventions in a row, in the order in which they were invented.One card starts on the table, and the starting player can choose any one of their cards and place it before or after the face-up card. Each player in turn does the same, placing cards before, after, or in-between cards.If a card is placed correctly, that player's turn is over. But if it was placed incorrectly (out of chronological order), that card is returned to the box and the player draws another.Once a round is over (every player has taken one turn), if a sole player has played their last card, they win. If 2+ players have played their last card, all player with cards remaining drop out, and the players with no cards draw a single card, and play continues until only one player has played their last card, and then becomes the winner.Exact knowledge isn't required to play this game. It will help, but guessing or estimating if an invention was made before or after other wise will likely be the main way non-historians will play. Over time and with repeat play sessions, players are likely to remember the years on the cards, and play will become easier.When this happens, add replayability by getting another Timeline deck and mix the cards up and the thrill of placing a card and the letdown of being off by a three years, or the thrill of placing a card right between where it belong, will refresh, adding new live to the game.Timelines: Inventions, as well as the other decks, are educational, and the game play is fun. This game is recommended for a filler game, as well as an educational activity.

reviewText: My little guy is four and has been obsessed with construction, its machines and its tools since he was about two. It works well indoors and I would imagine that it would be fun outdoors.  The size is good and it does what it is supposed to do.  I think any child who is into building, tools, and heavy equipment will enjoy this one

reviewText: The 654-piece Ravensburger KRYPT puzzle is a terrific solid-color jigsaw!  A long time ago, I put together a 500-piece, solid red, circular Springbok puzzle, but this was a lot more fun.  The Ravensburger puzzle puts a circle inside a rectangular puzzle shape, which makes the "picture"--and the challenge--quite interesting.  Also, there's a secret about the "circle" that you'll discover as you assemble the puzzle--just a little extra mental bonus.This puzzle, although difficult, is not nearly as difficult as some reviewers would have you believe.  Inside the box is a puzzle map--a line drawing that shows the shape and location of every single piece.  I made a photocopy (reduced to 75% of the original), and crossed each piece off (with pencil) as I found its location.  That way I didn't keep searching for the same pieces over and over again.With a puzzle like this, you must sort the pieces by general size and shape (e.g., oddly shaped, 2-tabs, 3-tabs, etc.).  I use clear plastic disposable dinner plates as sorting trays.  In this puzzle, there are many areas of different-sized pieces, which helps you assemble it--for instance,  the center pieces are much smaller than the rest, so it's easy to get started with them (as you do the border).  Every single piece has a unique shape, and most pieces will not fit together at all if they're not correctly placed.  If they are correct, the pieces slip smoothly into place without any forcing.It took me about 3 hours to complete the rectangular border, and about 20 hours (in sessions spread over 5 days) to finish the entire puzzle.  I always get kind of obsessed when I'm working a jigsaw, but I really enjoyed every minute of assembling this one.

reviewText: REPEAT PETE: CAN YOU DO WHAT PETE DOES WITHOUT MISSING A BEAT by Patch Products is a family board geared to children 8 and above. It comes with a board, pawns, a die, and Action and Special Action cards. The game itself is nicely constructed and very colorful and attractive. The rules are clearly written and easy to follow.Players simply draw an Action card and act out what the card shows. Then, the players move their pawn around the board. The next player draws a card and does the first action and then adds the action on their card, followed by moving their pawn. Players follow with everyone doing the actions in order and adding their action on to the end.Some of the Action cards have you imitate what is in a picture and some make you act like an animal. Some make you use sound and some are silent. Special Action cards give you choices. When someone forgets and misses something, players get a score for the cards they have and the losing player must roll the die for penalty points. Play then begins again until someone's pawn makes it around the game board to the end and they are the winner.This is a very silly game but both adults and children will enjoy it because it isn't complicated and it does involve everyone. REPEAT PETE gets players laughing at themselves and others, and everyone has a good time. Families would have fun watching everyone play. Be warned that people who can't laugh at themselves might not want to play this one...it takes a sense of humor and good self-esteem to carry this off, especially with "tweens" who worry so about what others "might think of them". The price might be a little steep for such a simple game but the materials are well made and would last a long time.

Play then begins again until someone's pawn makes it around the game board to the end and they are the winner.This is a very silly game but both adults and children will enjoy it because it isn't complicated and it does involve everyone. REPEAT PETE gets players laughing at themselves and others, and everyone has a good time. Families would have fun watching everyone play. Be warned that people who can't laugh at themselves might not want to play this one...it takes a sense of humor and good self-esteem to carry this off, especially with "tweens" who worry so about what others "might think of them". The price might be a little steep for such a simple game but the materials are well made and would last a long time.

reviewText: Games and toys should be chosen with specific personalities in mind. Some people might hate this game, but others will love it.I played it with a group of young adults who all enjoyed it very much. But it would be fine for younger players as well. I think anyone 8 or older could play it successfully.The game components are sturdy and well made. I highly recommend having one person study the extensive instruction booklet and summarize for the group.If you have played Tetris on the computer, you should be familiar with the concept for this game. Shaped pieces are placed on a platform to slide into place. Sounds easy enough. But the pieces must be added as certain cards are flipped. It's much harder than it sounds. And as the game progresses, you switch to different playing surfaces that have spots that should be left blank or covered up to add or subtract points from the player's score. It gets harder as it goes along.The game as designed is very challenging. But it's not a boisterous, laughing kind of fun game. It's more of a quiet, thinking game. Which can be great fun for the members of the family with good spatial thinking skills.This game may identify future architects and engineers and the less cerebral players may run screaming from the room.After playing it several times with seven different people, we all agreed that a smart math teacher could use the game components to create their own games for classroom centers to teach spatial skills and encourage thinking.Overall, a very enjoyable game but definitely in a different category from most board games I've played.
summary: Good quiet game for the thinkers in the family

reviewText: Tapple is a family word game designed for children ages eight and up and for 2-8 players. The object of the game is to name a word that is associated with a certain category. For example, the category may be "Things at the Beach." Once the category is announced, the timer is started and the first player has ten seconds to name something that would be associated with the topic category/phrase. Player 1 (we'll call him Bill) thinks of a word (sand), says it out loud, locates the letter "S" tab on the game wheel and presses it down. Once the "S" tab has been pushed down, it stays down until the end of the round, and signifies to every other player that no words beginning with "S" can be used again. Bill hits the large, red timer reset button in the center of the game wheel and passes the wheel to Sandy, who is on his left. Sandy blurts out a word (towels), presses down the "T" tab, hits the timer reset button, and passes it to Jeff, who is on her left. Jeff yells "Water!" and presses down the "W" tab. He hits the timer rest button and pushes the game wheel over to Mark, who is on his left.Play continues in this fashion until one of two things happen:1) A player makes a mistake and says a word beginning with a letter that is no longer able to be used (perhaps "seagulls," if following the example above).2) A player cannot think of a word to say before the timer runs out.Whenever either of these things happen, the player committing the offense is eliminated and cannot participate in the next round of play. A new topic card is selected and play begins again - ending in the elimination of another player. Rounds continue in this fashion until one player is left, and that player is the ultimate winner of the game.Rounds of this game go very quickly - rarely lasting more than two minutes. As such, playing a complete game from start to finish takes less than ten minutes, in most groups. Considering that this game is so short, it makes for a good filler game to try out between larger games with more depth.The manufacturer recommends players be ages 8 and up, and I think this is pretty accurate. My 6-year-old tried playing this game and was usually the first one eliminated. As kids get older and have a more expansive vocabulary, it will be easier for them to participate in this game. As far as the recommended number of players in this game, I would say that having more than six players is too many. Not every letter is available for use at the start of the game. with only 20 letters available, adding more players makes it even harder to compete - especially for the players who have to go last. I have played with up to six players, and I think 5-6 players is about what is ideal for this game.This is a pretty decent game that fills a niche for light, fast games in a family's game library. There is fun to be had, here, though you will have a hard time playing this game with younger children. Likewise, playing with a group of only adults will likely only last a round or two before players will feel like its time for something with more depth.*Edit: I am revising my score up to four stars from three. The reason for this is that my kids have been requesting we play several rounds of this game on family game night. They rarely do this with any game that we just played on the last family game night, but they are doing it with this game. Based on how much they enjoy it and their willingness to play it repeatedly, I need to give it a higher rating.

reviewText: My 7 year old is a Lego fanatic, so when we were given the chance to try out KRE-O sets, he was over the moon excited.The great things about these sets is the integrated parts that once assembled, allow the parts to move on their own. But this was a nice departure from the normal build and play. I think once built, this is great for younger kids that might not actually play with the toys once assembled.This set takes 3 triple A batteries which helps in making the people/ helicopter move. The attention to detail is fun for adults to check out and while some things (like tying off string and threading through small holes) aren't for kids tiny hands, my 7 rd old did most of the building himself. Not sure about longevity, but happy to have additional sets that can be used alone or integrated into our Lego family.

reviewText: My youngest son is a bona fide Thomas the Tank Engine fanatic, and we have tons of official trains, track sets, and take-n-play sets, in addition to other things like DVDs and books. So, he was interested in this toy, the "Thomas the Train: Take-n-Play Spills and Thrills" track set.The track components are made of a reasonably sturdy plastic, for the price range. Assembly was a little tricky ... my wife tried to assemble it, but the diagrams weren't clear in a couple of places. I ended up having to disassemble and reattach few pieces (which wasn't entirely easy to do as some aren't meant to be disconnected once connected) in order to get it together correctly.The toy is basically a downward leading track where the provided "Thomas" hits/triggers a few simple items on the way down (as you can see from the product pictures for this toy). The set doesn't stand up by itself ... you have to lean it against something. This helps reduce its overall footprint, for easy portability, but as a trade-off, you cannot fold this item up like you can most other take-and-play sets, so it still would take up a fair amount of space.The toy is rated for ages 3 and up. My son just turned 5, and he was bored by it after playing with for about 15 minutes. If you are getting this for a child, I would consider buying it for a 3 or maybe 4 year old; by 5 they've largely outgrown it. This isn't a bad toy, but it has fairly limited replay value. You could hook it up to additional track as part of making a larger train line, but even then, this is more of a supporting item than a "headliner" toy. Overall, I give this product three stars, which in my rating scale, equates to "ok".

reviewText: I got this game through the Amazon Vine program to review.  My five year old and I have played it together a number of times and it is a pretty fun game.Just a warning up front...you have to assemble all of the penguins.  It took my family maybe 15 mintues to do that, it's something you only need to do once.  My son actually got a kick out of building these penguins, so it wasn't completely a bad thing.The purpose of the game is to stack your penguins on the iceberg in such a way that they don't fall off.  The first person to get all their penguins on the iceberg wins.  Just be careful the iceberg swings and sways so you have to be careful not to knock off other penguins.  It you do they go into your pile.This is a super easy and quick game that is lots of fun.  Placing the penguins requires dexterity and also requires strategy.  You need to place the penguins in a way that they cause the least movement in the iceberg; it's an interesting lesson in balancing.  Also the slopes that you set the penguins on are diffrent steepness, so you have to figure out which steepness the penguins can sit on.  Also the direction the penguins face on the slope contributes to whether or not they will stay up there.So there's a lot of interesting physics involved but it's a very simple game.  The penguins are cute and when they fall off it's kind of funny.  There was a lot of laughing and giggling during this game.  Especially when the iceberg really got moving and the penguins were sliding and swaying.The only negative to this game is the dexterity involved. My son had a bit of trouble moving the pieces as carefully as me and my husband were able to.  Still there were a number of games he did win. reviewText: We bought one of these when my girls were just starting to pull themselves up. At the same time we bought another toy(Vtech Sit to Stand Walker) What a huge difference there is between the two toys safety.The Leapfrog Learning Table has always been very Sturdy, NEVER once has it tipped or caused my girls to fall. Even when both girls pull themselves up on the same side this stays put. When babies are learning to pull themselves up they need something sturdy. At first my girls would just stand in the same spot but before long they had learned to walk the entire table(while holding on) They can easily go from standing to a sitting position as well.The Vtech which is meant for going from sitting to standing was the most unstable toy ever. My girls were falling ALL the time so I finally just put that toy up permanently.This is something that my girls have played with every single day, several times a day since the day we first got it. Definately money well spend & it doesn't cost an arm & a leg.It is very durable so once your kids are done using it, you can sell it or give it to someone or keep it for future kids. The only thing I've noticed with not only our Table but with others is that the little door on it is easily pulled off but that is NOT a big deal at all. My daughters actually like pushing the button that was hidden under the door.If I had known about these sooner I would have gotten them when my girls were younger since you can take off the legs, you can put it on the floor or you can sit it on your lap or beside you while you hold your baby.This is one of the things I will & have recommended to any new parents.

reviewText: My daughter loves Polly Pocket, so this was a guaranteed winner before it even came out of the box. It's yet another colorful plastic thing for the kids. It is NOT freestanding, you are meant to attach it to the wall. It comes with the Command Strips for doing this, but personally I don't like sticking things up on the wall. The crank is supposed to operate the escalator and the Ferris Wheel, but only worked for the former. reviewText: My daughter absolutely loves this toy. She is 17 months old now and has been playing with it consistently from 2 1/2 months old. That is practically unheard of in this house. Most toys don't keep her interested for more than a week!Customization is easy. Violet's voice is friendly, upbeat, but not annoying. Songs are really short (I think my daughter's attention span can handle longer songs) and there isn't as much variety as I would like. My daughter likes them though. Sometimes she turns on Violet's music and then goes to play with other toys just because she likes to hear the music.This is one of the few toys we bring with us in the car, since its soft so if she throws it it won't damage our car, and probably won't hurt her if we were in an accident, but it also keeps her attention during the drive.She gets tired of Violet saying the same things and singing the same songs, so we customize her often. I'm glad its so easy to do since we have to do it a lot.I only wish Violet was easier to clean. Babies and toddlers are almost always sticky from food or something and get sick a lot. In order to keep Violet from getting too dirty or too germy we can only play with her at certain times. You can't throw Violet in the wash like other stuffed animals, and if you clean her with a cleaning solution you can't rinse her off. I spray her with Lysol disinfectant and let her air out for a good long while. So far she looks like new even though we've had her over a year.

reviewText: "I'm not sure how much more she can take!""Give her all you got, we're almost there!""You only have a narrow 2-3 second window to pull down the lever!"~And those were just from the adults in the room! Three adults (including myself) recently made one of the Hot Wheels cars with the 5-year old son of our friend. It was a HUGE hit, and both the cute little boy and the (somewhat cute) adults were excited and pleased with the end result.The product comes with OK instructions; we had to go to the hotwheels.com/carmaker site listed on the package to figure out why the door to the mold-making machine would not stayed closed, resulting in the annoying repetition of a computerized voice repeating "Error... error... error..."  Fortunately, the website (listed in the instructions) helped us resolve the problem (take out the wax stick, unplug it, and start over again).  Other than that, assembly was easy, fast, and without missing or non-fitting parts.You probably get the idea of how this works from the description and other reviews, so I'll be brief.  One places wax sticks at the top of the machine and waits for it to heat up (about 6-7 minutes), all the while watching lights flash and sound effect repeat.  This held the boy's attention for about 3-4 minutes; the adults tried to liven things up with the dumb jokes quoted above.  Once the mechanical voice announces that the machine is hot enough, depress the lever (within 2-3 seconds or who KNOWs what will happen! *smile*), and the waxy sticks melt into the car mold at that you've inserted at the bottom of the machine.  WAIT another eight or so minutes, and you'll hear that the cooling is complete and the door opens automatically.  This is VERY exciting after that waiting, but one still has to scrape off excess wax with the included plastic "tool" (if you lose this, many other objects will accomplish the same thing), loosen the now hardened car from the mold (not difficult), and then (easily) press it onto a prebuilt chassis, complete with working wheels. The waxen vehicle is richly colored (the purple has a very deep, almost metallic look; the finish does not look waxy or "cheap") and one finishes by adding decals onto the finished product. Oh, and then you get to play with it, too!The boy loved it, and held it in his arms when he left to go home.  HIs mom had to encourage him him to just lay it on the seat beside him as they drove home!A FEW THINGS YOU SHOULD KNOW.1. DEMANDING. This 5-year old, a very intelligent boy with precocious small motor skills, could NOT have done this himself.  Even after memorization of the instructions, the manual dexterity required (ESPECIALLY with the decals) is beyond his capabilities, and so Mattel is right: Suggested minimum age is 8, and even at that age, someone may need assistance.  Not that our "test subject" minded, he enjoys playing with adults, but you should take into account your child's need to do things "all by myself."2. PATIENCE.  Just making the mold requires about 15 minutes, minutes that go by very slowly when you're so anxious to see the finished product. Mattel  tried to accommodate this with the flashing lights and sound effects, but even this was not enough to distract our budding engineer.  The answer is...COOKIES!!!  I think the best way to play with this is to have a distraction/alternative activity going on while you're waiting... a book, a plate of cookies, etc.Adding the decals is fun, but adds another 35-35 minutes of focused effort. We let the boy try his hand at selecting and placing the decals, but ultimately it was the adults who put them on.  A 5-yearold might not mind; an 8+ year old might.3. MORE ABOUT THOSE DECALS.  They're tiny, they're not keyed to the different molds (figuring out which window decal, as just one example, fit which car model was something the adults had a lot of difficulty with), and Mattel could have easily printed some extra material on this.  We relied on the pictures on the package, but there was a problem here too:  Not only were just a few decals shown on the two car models, but decals were shown that are NOT included in the set! (It showed a white spoiler, for example, and there is no such decal included). What a shame-this was an unnecessary problem.4. What's Included. Despite these flaws, the toy makes beautiful hot wheel vehicles (one of them is a little more like a truck). You have enough wax to  make up to 10 molded cars, but can play with only three at a time because that's how many chassis are included. However, if you tired of one model, just snap it off, and replace it with one of the others. Additional wax can be bought (of course) if your youngster wants a fleet of vehicles or is a budding entrepreneur.5. Quality and Performance. The machine worked, the cars look excellent, and the decals (when finally applied) make them look exciting and realistic. The wheels are solid and the car rolls around well. For younger kids that don't mind getting help (and for parents and adult friends who don't mind giving it), you'll get fine results (but remember, patience and/or alternative activies will help!).6. Value. Too expensive, as are most toys. Even with the current $10 dollar discount it seems overpriced by 5-10 dollars. However, the fact that it works, that there's nothing quite like it (that I know of, anyway), and that individual hot wheels can cost quite a bit add to the value, as does the safety of the machine. Adult supervision will be necessary in most cases (in my opinion), but the machines was NOT hot to the touch.  Mattel, in its heartfelt concern about kids' safety (and equally since desire to not get sued) has a list of safety precautions about as detailed as if this were a chemistry set.7. Bottom line.  There's a LOT to like about this set, and few problems with getting it to work. The big issue is whether the manual and psychological (e.g., patience, cooperating with older peers or adults) demands will mesh well with your child's skill level and personality. I'd also like to see the price come down a little more, but our sample boy sure did love this!  Now, if they could make a similar set that makes other toys, perhaps include an activity while you wait, and have better guidance on those decals, Mattel would make a lot of kids happy, and have a new hit toy.

reviewText: A TRUE FAMILY OPPORTUNITY. This game can be played by pre-school child. What an opening for parents or grandparents to interact with children of their family or with others. If you like visiting at the senior center, take it along and you'll be the hit of the room. Everyone can play, and almost everyone knows how. That's why it's called classic. It will be classic and still played in the next century too.Anyone who has played knows that now matter how behind a player is, there is always the chance to regain momentum (or the opponents get Sorry-ied) and suddenly find themselves in the lead.Perhaps one of the greatest games available from the old-school (non-tech) realm that is educational, challenging, but above all, just plain FUN.This set is boasted to be retro-classic. It is in many ways. For one, the game has changed little since the invention of 1933, copyright Parker Bros. in 1934. My treasured 1939 copyright game has everything but the game board which came separate from the box with the cards and player pieces. The outside of the box looks almost identical to this new product, but the old box was only 4x7x1 inches. My instruction sheet is almost identical but a third the size as the new. So you see, the rules for "POINT SORRY!" are as old as the game itself. Another difference is the card back, while slightly larger in the 2013 Hasbro, and the old is blue, while the new is red. Of course the new cards indicate Hasbro.In the early version, the "men" or "playing pieces" were made of wood with stained colors of yellow, blue, red, and unstained natural. They were slightly smaller in size.
summary: Bottom line: BUY! You will not be SORRY!

reviewText: I just disassembled this and it is going back to the store where I bought it.  I ordered this because I wanted a sand and water table with an umbrella and liked that it had tracks for running cars around on.  The big thing for me was the umbrella though, since we are very fair skinned.  I read on another website the umbrella provided 30spf.  I find that hard to believe.  It was pretty big but quite thin and still allowed a lot of sun light through and of course only was effective if the table was at just the right angle to the sun (eg, the sun was directly overhead). I anticipate my son playing at times other than noon, so I don't see the point of keeping this table and getting one without an umbrella.  I will be getting the sand and water transportation station as it is a little smaller (for my 22 month old) and my plan was for this to go out on our balcony anyway.On a side note, one of the legs leaked.  I did read about this issue, and I'm sure I could've found a way to remedy it but combined with the umbrella issue it's just not worth keeping for me.  I think he'll like the bells and whistles on the transportation station table better, although I'm certainly not looking forward to what eventually becomes 8 layers of sunscreen throughout the day for us!  This just wasn't for us but I could see maybe if we had a big yard and I wasn't so concerned about the sun.  I really see no point in the umbrella though - it's just for show really.

reviewText: I remembered this game from my childhood, so I suggested when a family member was wanting to buy a gift for my preschool-aged children.  I would suggest other games in its stead.  This game does help with teaching counting as you add cherries to your bucket or subtract them depending on the spin, but there are other games that do this without some of the negatives I see in this game.First of all, I don't like that this game has exactly 40 cherries, 10 for each player.  As soon as one is lost, this is no longer a 4-person game, and given that this is a game for preschoolers and the cherries are tiny, losing one is almost a given.  I think an extra strip of 10 should be included.This is one of those games that's like the Bunny Hop.  However, it's more random and a lot less particular.  You have 2 cherries, then 3, then 1, then 5, then 7, then 0 and begin again.  I'd prefer a game that was a bit less random jumping all over the place.  And, it's not only occasional to be wiped out completely.  There's a 1 in 7 chance each turn of losing them all, and an additional 2 in 7 chance of losing 2.  There's really no way to tell if the end of the game is in sight, which can be frustrating for young children and their parents.Finally, there is a lack of logic in this game that bugs me.  If the dog or bird eats some of the cherries in your bucket or you spill them, then they go back on the tree.  How does that make more cherries grow on the tree?  With the game setup, this was kind of unavoidable, but still....The game is fine, but I almost never pull it down to play with my kids (5 of them ages 8 and under).  There are better ones out there, some of which we have, like Pengoloo or The Ladybug Game.

reviewText: So our family has younger kids, and trying to find games that even the 3 year old can play came sometimes be challenging.  Our latest game is Jenga, which now that we have used Suspend has very similar qualities which is probably why they like this too.  This game comes in a (flimsy) plastic tube that can somewhat be resealed, if you open it carefully on top.  Definitely the container could have been made more durable.  Then the pieces are made of medal, wood and a bit of plastic.  The general goal of the game is to balance as many of the pieces as you can, but if any of them fall on your turn, you take the pieces.  The person with the least pieces at the end wins.I do like that they outline in the instructions the different ways of playing, from beginner to intermediate.  In a lot of ways, you could make up your own versions of that depending on the number of people playing and the skill level.  I also highly recommend that if you have kids older than 7 you allow them to play by themselves a few times as well.  Gives them some strategies they can use once they join a group.I think the price is right on this one, but again, I probably would have paid a bit more for a descent case for this.
summary: A Nice Addition to Game Night with Kids

reviewText: Let me start out by saying, as a mom of an 8-year-old car crazy boy, this toy is very unique and a lot of fun, especially with more than one car at play. I didn't realize it initially, but these Kaotiks sets are actually expandable. You can put multiple sets together and create even bigger stunt parks. The pieces all disassemble and reassemble with ease, so keeping a box of parts for building is very convenient.We've had other toys like these with the cars that are supposed to go up and over ramps, but none of them have been very well executed. The ramps and jumps never stayed in place, the car didn't have enough speed to make an impressive jump, etc. Not so with Kaotiks. These cars are very very fast and are capable of performing some pretty amazing jumps and flips. My house is full of every variety of car toy imaginable, and this one shines as completely unique and a totally new way to have fun with RC cars. The play set and cars feel durable and have survived many, many flips, falls and crashes, so I have no worry of them breaking under normal play conditions.While performing 4 foot jumps at high speed is very entertaining, there's a fair bit of charge time here. My kids weren't upset about it as many of these types of toys work in the same way. They have about 8 minutes play time with 5 minutes charge time in between. We found that having multiple sets with multiple cars helped alleviate the downtime, and was also more fun when playing with multiple people. Crashing and competing with two cars is the most fun we have with these sets. The list price is a bit steep, but I've seen a few sales that made picking up a few sets much more affordable. At the right price, the Kaotiks sets are a lot of crazy fun!

reviewText: We do so many puzzles in our house, so I was interested to see how a puzzle storage system would work. This particular system is a large piece of felt and an inflatable tube.The felt is very durable and the pieces don't slide around, and the inflatable tube is a great toy for hitting other people with.The first couple of times I tried to roll up my puzzle and move it to another location, everything was fine with the rolling and unrolling, until I got to unrolling the last piece of felt that was around the tube. The puzzle pieces tend to slip out while the fabric is still on the tube, so the last five or six inches get ruined. A way to prevent this would be to keep a border of 6 inches on the edge that would be rolled first, so that part wouldn't be jumbled.Pros: you can (very carefully) move the puzzle successfully.the product is very sturdyCons: The puzzle pieces are not on a perfectly flat surface so the puzzle tends to buckle. I prefer a very flat surface for puzzling. There's a reason why I don't put puzzles on fabric.Bottom line: I wouldn't buy it again.

reviewText: Anyone that has ever bought anything even remotely associated with Disney knows that just having the Disney name on something means it will be more spendy than it otherwise should be.  Disney just doesn't tend to go cheap when it comes to their prices.  On the other hand, they may, at times, go cheap on the manufacturing quality (or the manufacturers that make the stuff for them may do so).  That may be in effect with this toy more than it should be.Truth be told, I think this could be an adorable item and it would certainly should be something that young girls that are fans of the movie Frozen would enjoy having and playing with, but the build quality is a bit flimsy (or perhaps the words there should say a bit more fragile than should be desired/expected) and it could lead to frustrations for the adults that would have to help support the younger users of the toy.The small Elsa doll/figure looks cute and it would certainly seem to be the kind of thing that would put a smile on a young girls face.  The only real concern that I would offer in saying that is that it is fairly small and could be a choking hazard for a family that had smaller children around.As a collectible display piece (for adults) this item could just be set up and left alone, and it would probably work just fine.  It would be more spendy than it should be, but it would still work for display.  As a toy that would be played with regularly, the fragile nature makes it somewhat less desirable.  If it isn't going to be durable, and won't hold up over time, it is harder to recommend for purchase.If you find it at a reduced price then by all means enjoy.  If your children just can't go without, then again, go for it, but expect you may soon enough hear some cries of disappointment because it has broken more easily than you had hoped.

reviewText: My mother loved playing Yahtzee, first with us kids and then with the grandkids. And the kids and the grandkids loved playing Yahtzee with mom even though she won all the time. Because of her love for the game I am pretty sure mom would have loved playing World Series of Yahtzee by Hasbrow.World Series of Yahtzee is a fast-paced, fast-action game in which everyone rolls the dice at once instead of taking turns and deliberately thinking about each move. Eight cards are turned up showing eight Yahtzee combinations, such as three sixes, three fours, full-house, small straight, four of a kind, etc.Everybody rolls and decides which of the eight combos to go for. The one who rolls their combo first, hits the buzzer to lock in their score. When the first player hits the buzzer, all other players are given five seconds to keep on rolling and come with a winning toss. The cards, each one with a point value, are collected by winning players at the end of each round the play begins again.You can play best three of five or play to see who gets the 10th win first. The set comes with one battery-operated buzzer unit (batteries not included), 20 dice, 22 game cards, one game board, four barriers and a game guide. You can play the game with two or four persons, age 8 and older.The only drawback is that two sets of dice have white dots and two sets have dark-colored dots. Mom would have had problems viewing the dark-colored dots which would put her at a competitive disadvantage. The kids and grandkids would be fine with that but mom would say it's not fair. And I would have to agree. You could pass the dark-dot dice around from player to player to spread the unfairness around. Or we could ask Hasbrow to put white dots on all the dice. Your call.But this game is so much fun that I'm not sure I will every play traditional Yahtzee again

reviewText: Both of my children (5 and 2) LOVE these blocks.  They will sit at the table and build "castles" and "towers" for an hour straight.  The box they came in is a good storage case, and the variety of shapes makes the possibilities endless.  Or would if we had 3 more sets of blocks.They are small, and will not stack well on carpet.  Using a hard stacking surface removes the "tumbling" frustration for us, except when one child wants to build and the other wants to demolish.  That's no fault of the blocks.  In my opinion, their size is great for the development of hand-eye coordination and finer motor skills.My only complaint, and the reason for 4 stars instead of 5, is that some of the paint has already begun to chip off some corners.  I am a little concerned about the long term durability, though I suppose that is purely a cosmetic issue and they will still stack even with chipped paint.

reviewText: TheDisney Sofia The First Vacation Palace Playsetis smaller than advertised in the listing.  The castle base (brown in the photo) is approximately 8 inches from the side of one turret to the far side of the other turret, and approximately 6 inches across the deck.  The mermaid lagoon is slightly bigger, at approximately 9 inches by 7.5 inches.I admit I was not an engineering major, but I had some difficulty assembling the castle. Some pieces some snapped in, so I know they were in correctly, but other pieces did not.  Anyone with large hands will likely have trouble maneuvering the small plastic pieces.  Furthermore, I strongly advise assembling it out of order - it is really difficult to attach the upper floors to the entrance AFTER the entrance is attached to the underwater base (step E), so I would try step G before step E.In addition to Princess Sophia and the castle, this set includes two pink chairs, a life preserver on a (plastic) rope, and a table. No other figurines are included. The steering wheel on the top level spins, and there is a slide as well as a turning wheel in the underwater level.  Princess Sophia's dress is removable, revealing her mermaid tail.I slightly prefer theDisney Sofia The First New Magical Talking Castlewhich wasn't quite as flimsy and was a little easier to assemble.It is unfortunate that Disney does not require better quality for licensed merchandise.

reviewText: Like many women my age, I fondly remember Easy Bake ovens and the little cakes that took a ridiculous amount of work to product a tiny cake that tasted only slightly better than cardboard. Fast forward 20 years and we have the NEW Easy Bake Microwave Delights. This set of cake decorating tools and cake/cookie mixes that are intended to be cooked via a microwave bear only a slight resemblance to the ovens we used, and clearly are a nod to the popularity of cake decorating shows like Ace of Cakes and Cake Boss. Who can resist the colorful, lovely miniature cakes displayed on the box? Not me, that's for sure! So how does this kit stack up?First off, opening the box and getting all the tools out is a task on its own, it took me about 15 minutes of work to get everything out. All laid out, it's an impressive array of tools, for baking the cakes and cookies, rolling out fondant, stamping and cutting tools, stencils, etc. I was impressed by the design of many of these, intended to make it as easy as possible for young girls to work with.Once I got to work though, I started to see some of the limitations. First, each cake mix makes 3 cakes, but the fondant only covers two at best. And that's if *all* you want is a single color per cake, which is rather boring. You'll quickly find out that to get the results on the box with many colors of fondant on different cakes, you'll use up pretty much all the packs that come with the set.The next problem is how fast the fondant dries out. It's really best if you have more than one person working to decorate as otherwise, you'll start getting dry, cracked fondant. While I didn't actually use a icing pack, the instructions do tell you to use one to fasten the decorations...so to do a fairly simple trio of decorated cakes, you're using up a cake mix, icing mix, and two fondant mixes. That's almost half of what you get when you buy it. Should you want to do cakes with more than just a couple colors, as shown in the ads, you'll pretty much use up all the fondant in one sitting.So if you buy this, prepare to run out of the baking mixes VERY fast. Refills can be very hard to find although I'd guess that someone on the internet are instructions for your own mixes to use with it. And maybe those might taste better as well...the results I got reminded me greatly of the fairly tasteless cakes of old. Not quite as bad, but still not something I care to bother eating again (or the effort in involved in making them). The layer of solid sugar (i.e. fondant) only made things worse for me, but young girls still will probably be proud of their cake decorating results using this kit. Should you be able to find other ways to use all the tools it comes with, it may indeed be worth purchasing. For me, it was a fun trip done memory lane, but not quite what I hoped for. See the photos I posted for a view of all the decorating tools, and a sample of the cakes I was able to make....somewhat underwhelming compared to the ones on the box and not much to show for nearly an hour of work.

reviewText: I got the Playskool Poppin Park Learn N Pop Lion from Amazon Vine, as I thought it would be something my 16 month old would like. He is very much into animals right now and has started counting (with help), so it seemed perfect.When we opened the package, he was really excited and signed 'lion' and roared a bunch of times. The lion comes with 3 balls that work with other Playskool poppers (we don't have any). The "frustration free" packaging is a step up from the old twist-tie system but still takes longer to open than a toddler has patience, so my recommendation would be to open it before your child is around. The lion's face moves up and down (why, I'm not certain; different tunes don't play, and the face has to be open in order to put balls inside). Kids place a ball in the lion's mouth, triggering a mechanism, and the ball is counted. Pulling the tail "pops" the balls out (so does knocking it to the side) and plays a little song or the lion roars or yawns.Pros:* On the cover of the instructions, it tells you it's set on demo mode, and you need to switch it to 'on' for all functionality. I've been duped by that before!* Comes with AA batteries already installed* Can count up to 10 in English, Spanish, French, and Mandarin.* Setting the language to a specific language is very easy. Changing it is also easy. Remembering how to change it once you've lost the instructions? Perhaps a little more difficult. It seems like it could've been imprinted on the plastic.* Instructions also contain a pronunciation guide for the languages.Cons:* AA batteries included only lasted about a week before needing to be replaced.* Whether he played with it on the floor or on a table (at his height or higher), he kept knocking the lion over on its side. It's very lightweight, and it doesn't work on the side.* Notice in the picture that there are 2 balls inside the lion and one outside? That's because there's only room for 2 balls in there. Not very friendly for storage or trying to keep pieces together.* Makes a weird noise (gulp, yum, mmm) before the number. I could see kids adding in this sound, thinking it's how you pronounce the number.* Kids have to be shown how to work it, especially if the face is down. There's no voice saying "Lift my mouth and feed me balls" or helping the kids work through the process on their own.He plays with it for maybe 5 minutes at a time before he gets distracted. He also has the counting Cookie Monster and he LOVES playing with that. If it had space for 10 balls in the lion's back, I think that would improve the amount of time he spent - he's got to realize that you keep feeding the balls back into the mouth. Because the counting time resets, if the balls are popped out across the room, he has to chase them and get them back to the lion to continue in the series. It has never happened.Overall, I don't see this being a long-term toy that we keep; it doesn't hold his attention, tips over too easily, and makes the weird sound before naming the number. If it didn't also include French and Mandarin, I'd give this 2 stars.

reviewText: "Did you ever play Tic-Tac-Toe?""Yeah, of course.""But you don't anymore.""No.""Why?""Because it's a boring game...it's always a tie."That conversation is from the 1983 movie War Games...and it perfectly sums up my feelings on the board game Urban Myth.HOW TO PLAY THIS:It sounds simple enough, the goal is to travel around the city blocks and collect letters with correct answers to questions that are either truths or myths. But it can get confusing pretty quickly.One person is the card reader, which changes after each turn. A question is read, and the other players vote with their Truth/Myth cards. The players advance one square for everyone who guessed correctly. If a player doesn't guess correctly, they cannot move.If no one gets the question right, the card reader moves one space for each incorrect answer. (Confused yet?)If a player gets a question right and the category on the board matches the category being read on the card, the player gets to move AND keep the card. Whoever spells TRUE or MYTH first is the winner.OUR REACTION:First, The Truth/Myth cards aren't very sturdy - they are weaker than the deck cards and have a greater chance to get creased or ripped.Next, it's common with trivia board games to have a goal to reach while moving the pieces around the board...but that doesn't happen here. You keep going around the same bland board over and over in different city blocks, trying to collect letter cards. Moving the pieces feels kind of unnecessary, to be honest.We noticed some of the questions were phrased in such a way that the answer was pretty obvious. For example:"The premier of the ill-fated X-treme Football League was the least-watched event in the history of prime-time network programming."The use of "ill-fated" in the question leans toward a "true" answer. If the question simply said "The premier of the X-treme Football League was the least-watched event in the history of prime-time network programming", that would be more vague and a little harder to guess.We also felt some of the questions were out of place for younger players, such as the ones below:"An Oklahoma City rapist was sentenced to 30,000 years behind bars.""Iranian women are enrolling in American microbiology classes in order to build biological weapons of mass destruction for release in the U.S.""A man known as 'Slavemaster' on the internet has murdered 56 women and is the focus of an FBI manhunt.""Illinois senator Barack Obama is a Muslim radical."And the crown jewel:"Action star Sylvester Stallone's first role as a leading man was in a 1970's porno flick."Finally, the majority of this game (for us, anyway) was spent breaking ties. When two players qualify to keep a letter, the Card Reader draws another card and asks another question until only one person gets the question right. Some of the questions have very obvious answers, so these ties kept happening over...and over...and OVER. Ties could have been broken MUCH easier by including a single die and having the two players choose a number.All in all, this game was okay...it did have some interesting questions and sparked a few conversations, but we got bored very quickly because every other question ended up as a tie.Fun, but for a limited time.
summary: LOTS of ties, some inappropriate questions, and so-so gameplay.

reviewText: Chalks are easier to review. Few simple things differentiate between the dollar store and good ones. Color contrast, washability, consistency are the main parameters. reviewText: So says my five-year-old daughter who has watched every "My Little Pony:  Friendship is Magic" episode multiple times and who owns the world's largest collection of Ponies on earth.  Well, maybe I exaggerate, but the Ponies do seem to be everywhere in our house.  She was so excited by this toy that she immediately tried to set it up herself.  I've hardly been able to get her to bed or out of the house since.  Her three-year-old sister, also an avid Pony fan, elbows in her fair share of time too.Not being an avid Pony fan myself (although, as far as such entertainment goes, it is one of the better shows), I'm not as enamored of this toy as the girls are, but it's decent.  It assembles rather intuitively without too much need for the instructions and, what's better, no tools or batteries are required.  The structure is fairly simple.  A curved staircase leads up to an open platform.  Underneath the platform are a Pony-sized swing and a drawbridge leading to a small chamber, while on top are little minarets, one big enough to have a balcony-type platform.  The "castle" is decorated with flags, trumpets and a butterfly and can be further decorated with stickers that are rather difficult for little hands to apply.The set also comes with two Ponies, Princess Cadence and Shining Armor, as well as a host of small to practically microscopic accessories, including clothes, rings, crowns and the like for the two Ponies, and a wedding cake, chandelier, bouquet, table, piano, teapot and teacups for the castle.  I know it's only a matter of days before those teacups are going to end up missing, that is, until they turn up again under my heel at 3:00 o'clock some morning.  I can't figure out why toy companies design such small pieces for such little kids.  Aside from the likelihood of pieces getting lost, however, this set seems pretty durable.This toy doesn't have a lot of bells and whistles.  Aside from the swing and the drawbridge, there are no moving parts (well, the flags and the butterfly are adjustable, but it's pretty minor).  Most of the action will have to come from your child's imagination (or memory of the show).  That doesn't seem to be a problem for our girls, who have been holed up, either alone or together, playing with this toy for days now.  Recommended for the little Pony lover in your family.

reviewText: My Daughter and I have been working on a 3000 piece puzzle for over a month. I then inflated the tube which by the way reminded me I'm no spring chicken any-more!  That done I placed the tube onto the end of the felt as shown on the box and began to roll. It may be better than nothing but I don't like it.  The felt mat however is wonderful both in size and it keeps the pieces from sliding around as you are working on it; for that I give it two stars.The concept is great but it simply doesn't work for me.
