reviewText: My 2, 6 and 8 year olds have been having a blast with this dollhouse since I put it together the other day.  I'd say the 8 year old has probably enjoyed it the most of the three!Assembly was very simple.  A couple pieces to screw on.  A secret playroom that was a little tricky to get in place, but maybe that was just me.  A cleverly hidden battery compartment that requires a couple of AAs.  And some stickers to apply around the dollhouse.  I think it probably took 15 minutes to put together at most.The dollhouse isn't as durably made as some of the younger Fisher Price toys.  The plastic feels a little flimsier.  But having assembled various Barbie dreamhouses, boats and planes, I can say it seems sturdier than some other competing products.  There aren't a lot of extra pieces for the kids to lose which is a huge plus.  The house doesn't have a lot of snapped in parts to break and fall off.  The doll family is very well put together and fun for the kids.  This is a toy for the imagination.Last comment is that I like how the dollhouse folds up easily and doesn't take up a huge amount of space when play is over.  The dolls all fit inside, and the house folds up neatly into a corner.  Goes from a nice sized house to compact storage very easily.I'm sure your younger girls will enjoy this dollhouse as much as mine.

reviewText: I don't know what it is, but I just can't drink the Kool-Aid when it comes to Days of Wonder's "Small World."  Don't get me wrong, I think it's a decent game and many of my friends really enjoy it.  It is well designed and relatively well balanced.  I guess I just don't get why it's supposed to be fun.Players take on the role of a difference and unique race by combing characteristic cards with race cards.  This I do like, customizing a new race every time you play.  The different abilities can be a lot of fun, especially if you put them together in fun and imaginative ways.  Half of the setup you'll be laughing at the odd combinations you and your friends are able to put together.  From there, however, it really goes downhill.  You place units of your race all over the board, as do your opponents.  The more spaces you occupy, the more revenue you gain.  Since you are limited in how many spaces you can ultimately claim by the number of units available to you, you will eventually want your race to go into decline.  This allows you to claim board spaces for a younger and more energetic race, while still controlling spaces for your previous race- until they are overtaken by others.  Simply put, this is a game of area control that doesn't have a whole lot going for it other than its silly theme- and that wears really thin after a while.  One of the reasons I don't really care for this game is how conflict is resolved.  Essentially anyone can take a space from another player, provided they have more units than their opponent.  It's a form of determinative combat that really takes all of the thrill and fun out of conflict.  True, under certain circumstances players can roll a dice to possibly add a few points to their roll, but the defender does not roll, and the result is just a generally bland combat experience.As I said above, I do not think "Small World" is a bad game, it's just really not my cup of tea.  Many people do love it, but I just don't get it.  In my opinion Days of Wonder has produced some truly top notch games like "Mystery of the Abbey," "Memoir '44," and the absolute gem "Shadows Over Camelot."  If you're looking for a great board game experience, I highly recommend any one of those before "Small World."
summary: Not a Bad Game, Just Not One of My Favorites

This allows you to claim board spaces for a younger and more energetic race Simply put, this is a game of area control that doesn't have a whole lot going for it other than its silly theme- and that wears really thin after a while. One of the reasons I don't really care for this game is how conflict is resolved. It's a form of determinative combat that really takes all of the thrill and fun out of conflict. True, under certain circumstances players can roll a dice to possibly add a few points to their roll, but the defender does not roll, and the result is just a generally bland combat experience.As I said above, I do not think "Small World" is a bad game, it's just really not my cup of tea. Many people do love it, but I just don't get it. In my opinion Days of Wonder has produced some truly top notch games like "Mystery of the Abbey," "Memoir '44," and the absolute gem "Shadows Over Camelot." If you're looking for a great board game experience, I highly recommend any one of those before "Small World."

reviewText: I chose this playset for my 3 year old daughter.  She is a huge horse fan, so I knew she'd enjoy it.  I was right.  She really loves playing with the unicorn.  The wings can be flapped and she really likes putting shoes (you get 4 blue ones and 4 purple ones) on the unicorn.  In addition, she likes the hair barrettes.  This set also comes with a cape (hard to put on because you have to get it under the wings and also secure it closed - parents need to do this because little fingers aren't dexterous enough), jewels that can be used to decorate the cape, two tiaras (I need to help my daughter with the tiara), a little plastic hair dryer, a telescope, a treasure chest, two sets of books, and a miniature perfume bottle.  Accessories are cute but they don't all fit in the treasure chest or the drawer in the vanity in the palace.  We are using a little box that we have for storage.  Otherwise, the numerous small pieces will get lost.The crystal palace itself requires assembly.  It comes in a few pieces that snap together and you have to add a few stickers.  It doesn't feel very secure. Also the playset doesn't add much to the play.  It comes with a few hangers, but nothing really hangs on them.  The vanity has a small drawer, but it isn't big enough for storage.  There is a ramp to a second level, but the pony barely fits on the second level of the palace and there isn't much to do.The best part of the set is the unicorn because her wings flap.  The shoes are great too and easy for a three year old to manage, as is the little hair dryer and telescope.  Everything else requires a bit more dexterity that an older child would have (e.g., ages 6+) but this set doesn't engage older children as much unless they are die-hard MLP fans (my older girls are not).Overall, it's cute but could definitely be better.

reviewText: I bought this kit along with the Melissa & Doug doctor kit (Melissa & Doug Doctor Role Play Costume Set). The reason I bought both was to be sure I got all the tools I wanted, and the M&D; kit had the doctor's coat and surgical mask.I really like all of the tools that came with the Fisher Price kit, except the stethoscope, which is sad because that's one of the main reasons I bought two kits. The M&D; stethoscope is also strange to use. The Fisher Price stethoscope is too stiff to be used "properly" and isn't comfortable in my ears (I assume it isn't in my child's ears, either.) Both of my kids (ages 3 and 1) really like the syringe ("medicine shot," as they call it) and the band-aid. My son really likes the blood pressure cuff (the M&D; kit did not have one) and I found that the velcro was actually suitable for an adult's arm, but not a child's. It would be an easy fix if I wasn't too lazy to glue some more velcro on the band.The storage bag only closes at one point with a small piece of velcro, but even when I combine the Fisher Price tools and the Melissa & Doug tools in the bag, it still closes just fine. Once the pieces are put away, I usually store the bag on a shelf, so the items spilling out has never really been an issue.I'm hesitant to fully recommend this kit, as I don't think I would be satisfied with it had I not also bought the Melissa & Doug kit to make up for anything missing. In fact, I'm not sure that I'm fully satisfied with either kit! Both kids really enjoy playing with the tools, so I guess that's what counts. I would love a better stethoscope, though!

reviewText: This is one of my favorite family games.  It can easily be played by a large number of people, which is always a good thing.  Essentially, in this game each player is given seven "red apple" cards, each of which has a noun on it, such as "a school cafeteria," "the FBI," or "sharks."  Each card also has a little bonus description or joke, such as "many species living today are similar to those from 100 million years ago.  Because change is scary."  Each round, a different player is "it," and flips over a "green apple" card, which ahs an adjective on it, such as "hardworking," "foreign," or "shy."  The other players each choose on of their noun cards they feel the "it" player will choose as being the best match for the flipped-over adjective.  The player whose "red apple" card is chosen keeps the "green apple" card- first player to reach a certain number of green cards wins.This game is a lot of fun- it has next to no set up and can easily be transported without the box if the occasion arises.  Works well with large or small groups, and with people you know well or are getting to know.  It is a really good buy.

reviewText: The Bop-It XT is an interesting twist on the original Bop-it Game. I played the original game and liked the simplicity, believing that was difficult. I also enjoyed the sound effects for your score. Bop-It XT is way more evolved than that and all of the other extreme versions. It is definitely more lightweight than the other Bop-It XT. I think this is a great feature for children and adults because it is easier to hold and great for travel. I like the new addition to XT, which is the Shake It option. Not only is there a pull-it, bop-it, twist-it, flick-it, and spin-it, but there is also a shake-it. You do not have to touch this one, but rather shake the whole game, which makes it more fun. You also do not have to use the shake-it option. If you do not press on it, it will not come out and the announcer on the game will not call it out as an action to perform. I think the choice makes the more appealing to customers because they have a choice; I know I was more intrigued.The game speaks a lot more than it used to and there are many options. There is the solo option, pass-it option, party option, and one-on-one option. More ways to play keeps the game interesting over and over. It also speaks loud and clear and you can change the volume. This is a great edition; for example, if a child brings the game on a long road trip. The game turns off quickly when not in use to not waste batteries and actually states that it is turning off. It also tells you to play when you pull the pull-it to start it. It is efficient for all ages. It also states your score after you lose and makes comments based on how well you did. All comments are family-appropriate and mildly humorous.If I had any complaints, I would say that it looks cheaply made compared to past games. It does seem to hold up and work well though. I also think for the Bop-It game, it starts off too fast to begin. I have not gotten very far yet to see how fast it goes, but I do believe it should start off a little slower. This way, small children can get to play for a little while before losing as well. I also believe it is very similar to the past games, with mild adjustments. I think modern updates are necessary every once and a while, but I think Bop-It XT should suffice for a while. Overall, it is an entertaining game with effective announcing and parts. I would recommend this game to people who enjoyed the original Bop-It game and new-comers who want a challenge for fun!

reviewText: It is hard not to love a Reiner Knizia game!The objective of the game is to score points based on completing shapes that score points while avoiding combinations that subtract points.  The game is played in rounds.  Each round a different scoring convention is added to the game.  In the first round, the scoring for general shapes, regardless of color are introduced.  In the second round a complication is added when specific shapes of a particular color join the first criteria, and in the third round shapes that detract from your score are introduced.  The scores from all three rounds is added (you could have a negative score from the third round) to determine the winner.There is an optional fourth round where larger, scoring, colorless shapes are introduced.The game pieces are very durable, and the assembly of the components the first time is easy.Here is the Dr. Games evaluation:GO/NO GO criterion* Complexity: Bits scores moderately well on this one. The game plays at two levels of complexity. There are only 48 possible scoring combinations on the easy level and 192 scoring combinations for the advanced game.The rules are relatively straight forward, but not everyone has a good spatial sense.  Some players will find this game to be frustrating, because you have to anticipate where future shapes may "fall."  Bits is complex in the same way that Chess or Go are complex.  While the rules are simple, visualizing the future is a big part of the game, and some players may find that challenge daunting.The game is rated as being suitable for eight year olds.  I did not find this to be true.  When I played it with four 8-10 year olds, the only one that "got" the game was a little boy who plays a lot of Playstation DS(tm) games that require spatial understanding.  The other three sat through three games with a lot of encouragement, but I doubt any of the three could be persuaded to play again.Conversely, I also play tested the game with my group of "twenty-somethings," who are all engineers or computer science folks, and they liked the game a lot.My best estimate is that this is a 15+ year old game.* Balanced: Anyone can win or lose, but there are certain skills or lack thereof that can make this game challenging at best.  If you do not have a strong ability to visualize spatial relationships then this game will prove a challenge.  It would be similar to playing Set with a group of color blind players.  Yes, it is balanced, unless you don't have the spatial thinking gene.* Chance: Bits has the appropriate level of chance.  The specific scoring changes from game to game in a random way.  The sequence of tiles drawn is random, but is the same for everyone.  The game ends up being predominantly about strategy and visualizing potential future tile placement..* Clarity: The rules are clear and understandable in a single reading.* Reasonable Time: Once you know the rules, you can play a game from start to finish with four players in less than 30 minutes.BONUS criterion* Social: Not so much ... Bits is less conducive to socializing than many games.  The kids talked during the game about things outside of the game, mostly because they found the game a challenge to play.  The twenty to thirty year old crowd talked about the game, but not about what was going on in the game.  Folks that had trouble visualizing tile placement talked about the weather, cooking, and kids.* Unique/interesting Mechanic: The idea of different patters being worth more positive or even potentially negative points is very clever.* Inform: There is not a lot of educational value.  Our experience with the game is that it is more of "an IQ test for spatial recognition" than a way to learn about it.* Rewards Throughout: Each round has scoring.  That is a nice way of creating waypoints in the game.If you have a techie group of friends, college or post-college, this is a good game to pick up as a change of pace.As Reiner Knizia games go, this is not one of his classics, but it is worth buying and playing to round out the family game closet.In service,RichThe Original Dr. Games since 1993

reviewText: While simple in concept, Indigo is a fun family game that's different every time you play. Between two and four players use playing tiles to create a path for their token to follow, getting it from its starting place to another place on the game board. The 54 route tiles make sure that every game is unique. Players can build alliances with opponents to advance, but there's only one winner. As players lay the connected tiles, they build intricate pathways that utilize both strategy and luck in advancing their token. The game features a game board, 24 glass gemstones, 24 player tokens, 54 route tiles, 7 treasure tiles, and four privacy screens. the game takes about 20-30 minutes and is appropriate for ages 7-99.

reviewText: We obtained this toy for our three kids (3, 5, and 6 years old).  All of them love camping and we thought the campfire log would nicely complement the kid's tent in the play room.  The toy log is a great idea, and executed well with solid materials, long battery life, and realistic appearance.  But there are two flaws that detract from it; 1.) the cloth flame often gets stuck in the base; and 2.) the motor's noise level is too loud.  Also, the button that activates the flame shuts off too quickly (10 seconds or less).Product Strengths:- High quality design and materials at an affordable price.- Great durability - it's survived 6+ months in our playroom with no problems.Product Weaknesses:- Loud motor noise level for blowing flame - Hearing the mechanical sound doesn't bring back memories of being around a campfire.- Cloth flame gets stuck in base.  This takes lots of dexterity to fix and often requires parent effort.- Power button shuts off device too quickly.  For longer use, there's an on/off button, but it doesn't turn off the toy automatically.- Limited application - kids quickly grow tired of and it's use around the house is limited.Overall, would we purchase this as a gift for another child?  - Probably not.  As one reviewer indicated, the noise level is the toy's fatal flaw.

reviewText: Playskool's "Big Hugs" Elmo is the best iteration of this doll to date.  Standing almost 2 feet tall this doll is best suited for kids aged 2+ and up (even though the product's recommended age starts off at 18 months).  This latest version of Elmo is a clear evolution of previous models due to new features such as physical actions like motorized hugs, dance movements and gyroscopic responses (eg - see what happens when you hold him upside down).  There is also a good variety of spoken responses (50), songs that will be sung and a sleepy-time mode that will help put youngsters to sleep.  Durability seems decent provided your youngsters don't manhandle Elmo too excessively.  Requires 4 AA batteries (not included) and after 2 weeks of frequent usage by 2 kids the power seems to be going strong.  Overall, a fun and well designed product that is sure to become a new 'best friend' for those lucky enough to receive this.

reviewText: My daughter purchased this kitchen set for her 16 month old son. I volunteered to assemble this kitchen set. It arrived in a carton weighing 75lbs. The only other tool needed for assembly is a phillips head screwdriver.The unpacking was done last night in a spare upstairs unused room. It is best to do this assembly without any small children around to pick up any small parts.At 9AM on a Saturday morning I was ready to begin.The instructions are all pictures making assembly easy but although I am fairly handy it took me until 4 PM to complete this assembly. This included a few short breaks as well as a lunch break and a little play time with my grandson.After the small parts were installed on the larger pieces, the large pieces were carried downstairs to be assembled in the play room. It was worth every minute of my time to see the happy excited look on his face when he finally began to play with it.Highly recommended.Howard in New Jersey

reviewText: I have to say that I had never heard of Beyblade before this.  As soon as I got this home, my sons (8 and 10) took over.  They had a blast!  Basically, this is a simple battling tops toy.  There are some rules other than "last man standing" for point scores, but the basic idea is that whoever's top is still spinning last wins.  The tops come apart to be customized (although this is a starter kit, so you'll have to buy more stuff it you want to customize) for performance characteristics.  I have to admit that I don't see any differences in the way the tops perform, but my sons do.  They've already started planning more purchases in this line, and I have had to add Beyblade to the DVR (there's a cartoon to go with this).About the only negatives I can add are these.  The arena is pretty flimsy.  Very thin and flexible plastic.  It looks like it would break very easily, but as long as no one leans on it or stacks anything on it, it should last.  Likewise, the ripcords appear flimsy too, but they are holding up so far.  Second, I would not recommend this for really young children.  It is not that it might be a choking hazard, but the tops are mostly die cast metal and they are going pretty fast.  There is the potential for injury with very young children.  The instructions warn against leaning on the arena while the tops are in play, and your children need to be old enough to understand that a metal top in the eye could cause some damage.

reviewText: It's truly amazing how something so simple can be so great. This product performs the tasks of scissors with the ease of an X-acto knife. However, unlike the X-acto knife, you really don't have to worry about cutting a finger or any other major safety concern. The general uses of this product are to cut wrapping paper, coupons, and magazine pages for recipes or cataloging. In essence, anything that is paper, and doesn't require great precision this product is excellent for you. If you need more precision than a sloppy straight line, you're better off using scissors. I did want to see what else I could use this product on, so here are my results...Parchment paper = works excellent if you don't mind waxy build up on the blade.Fabric = Um, no unless you like your fabric with a fine snagged look.Kitchen foil = It works, but you have to imagine that this increases the rate that the blade dulls.Document envelope opener = ExcellentIn summation, this product can't really equate to the usefulness of scissors. However, if you're really into crafts and/or a lot of gift giving. Then this little tool will be perfect for your craft tackle box.

reviewText: This product appears to be the successor to theCrayola Crayon Maker.  In that regard, I was hopeful as that unit left a lot to be desired.  This unit is not much improvement.As others note, the toy is great in concept just poor in delivery. Assembly is fairly straight forward though you need your own light-bulb (not supplied).  Next, have you ever used a light-bulb to melt crayons?  Neither did I.  Let me tell you its not a fast process and you will have to explain this fact to your child, but you can use the 25 minutes it takes to melt crayons to do this.  This method is clearly a necessary safety precaution similar to an EZ-Bake oven. The kids loved the concept and choosing colors however and turning the knobs on the machine.  However, if you turn one of the knobs, the automatic child lock engages and you will need to wait until it disengages.The kids loved to watch the crayons melt and though it was really cool to reuse crayons destined for the trash bin. However, after experimentation, I would not mix the cheaper crayons (like those from restaurants) with crayola's. It seems there is a difference in the wax used and the two mix horribly and melt at different temperatures. Cleanup is a little difficult and will require you do some scraping, but overall no big deal.I suspect most people will be happy with the project IF they have patience.  I would say it is a perfect rainy day toy for parents and children (8 and under).

reviewText: I think this is an extremely well-done, subtle robot toy. It is a baby primate (orangutan?) that makes little cooing sounds and gestures, sucks on a bottle, wiggles a bit if you press a few spots, and not much else. It really appears to be alive though--it blinks every few seconds, makes slight movements with its head and shoulders--and I find myself mesmerized by it. Philosophically, I like the fact that it doesn't put on a big song and dance and allows a child to interact with it in an open-ended way. However, my 2.5 year-old daughter doesn't show the slightest interest in it. She glances over for a moment when I turn it on and then resumes playing with her inanimate dolls. I guess she prefers to completely project her imagination onto her toys without any interference from robotics.

reviewText: I'm a father of two and my 7-year-old daughter loves Barbie dolls. The Barbie Fairytale Royal Doll set is, as the images show, a basic 3-piece Barbie set that includes a fairy Barbie, princess Barbie, and mermaid Barbie.Interestingly, all three dolls in this set feature the same "winter pattern" of snowflakes so I suspect this set will be heavily promoted in stores around the holidays. Like most Barbies, the dolls themselves are pretty durable but the accessories (crowns, dresses, wings, etc.) are less so. The top parts of the winter clothing on these dolls are actually molded on, so those parts of the outfits are VERY durable but it's also a little odd if you're used to the "classic" Barbies with clothing that can be completely changed.The main advantage of a three-piece set like this is the price is roughly the same as buying two Barbie dolls (assuming you don't buy your Barbie's during closeout sales). So, if you're an adult looking for a Barbie-themed gift for a child and want to know you got a good deal then this set is indeed good value for your money.

reviewText: Does Barbie need another RV?  Probably not.  However, this new Pony Tale RV is pretty neat if you're a first timer, like myself.  This RV comes with multiple accessories and can change depending on how many dolls you are playing with.  All the pieces into the camper so that when you eventually pull the camper apart, it forms a large play area that includes a kitchen, bedroom area and bathroom.  Not only is this an RV, but it is also a four person vehicle if you detach the front from the back pieces.  Unlike the Barbie Dreamhouse, this was very simple to put together.  It took very little set up time.  There are stickers involved, though, which might take a few minutes depending on how you are with those.  The RV rolls well and seems to withstand creative play well.  I should also point out that this isn't a small playset-- it's small enough to store, but isn't 'too' small that the dolls seem giant.Also included is a pool/fire pit.  As a pool, the separate accessory isn't fantastic.  As a fire pit, however, it is kind of neat!  Surprisingly, the pool fits very well into the RV when packed up.  Mattel did something genius when designing the major pieces of furniture in this RV. The tables and counters have circles that are designed to hold the small accessories (cups, plates, food stuffs).  While I still pack them in a sandwich bag when not being used, for creative play, the fact that the accessories don't fall all over the place is fantastic.Overall, this is a pretty nice Barbie accessory, regardless of if it comes with a Pony (for the A Pony Tale tie in) or not.  It looks like it should be pretty useful for doll photoshoots and for creative play.

Unlike the Barbie Dreamhouse, this was very simple to put together. It took very little set up time. The RV rolls well and seems to withstand creative play well. I should also point out that this isn't a small playset-- it's small enough to store, but isn't 'too' small that the dolls seem giant.Also included is a pool/fire pit. As a pool, the separate accessory isn't fantastic. Surprisingly, the pool fits very well into the RV when packed up. Mattel did something genius when designing the major pieces of furniture in this RV. The tables and counters have circles that are designed to hold the small accessories (cups, plates, food stuffs). While I still pack them in a sandwich bag when not being used, for creative play, the fact that the accessories don't fall all over the place is fantastic.Overall, this is a pretty nice Barbie accessory, regardless of if it comes with a Pony (for the A Pony Tale tie in) or not. It looks like it should be pretty useful for doll photoshoots and for creative play.

reviewText: I can't believe how great this playhouse is. My almost-two-year old daughter loves it. The house comes with three people figurines (a mommy, daddy, and baby), as well as a car and some other extra little accessories. There is a ton to do inside the house. There are five or six different listening stations, where you can hear Daddy and Mommy sing, do dishes, flush the toilet, make a phone call, etc. The sounds can be changed if you switch the house from day- to night-time mode.I really like how durable all of the pieces are. Everything feels very solid and substantial. The pieces that need to stay together do, and the extra pieces seem to fit perfectly in my daughter's hand.My only gripe is that if you move the house too much (and we've moved ours A LOT), the batteries, located on the underside of the toy, can shift around and cause the sounds to stop playing. If you shake the toy around again, it is easy to knock things back in place, but it is still kind of annoying.Regardless, my daughter loves this playhouse, and I am very happy with it, overall.

reviewText: As an adult, I really appreciate the design of the game - using the box as the board, using the control tower to roll dice, etc. The pieces, specifically, the plane is also well-designed (time will tell how it will stand up to many hours of play). reviewText: The toy, as is, is OK, the kids love it and they play with it a lot. It's educational, the games and books are appealing, it's interactive, they're building new neural pathways in their brains, and they sit and play for hours at a time.The main problem is the downloadable content. We've finally gotten the free stuff and we've tried paying for stuff, and it is really hard to get the download going and keep it going. I think that of all the things we've tried to load we've only succeeded once, I gave up and my husband finished it, I think we got all of the free stuff. Since then we've just been trying fruitlessly to duplicate that random success.I download a lot of stuff every day, (ask amazon, they know how many tv shows, downloadable games, and free kindle books I've gotten from them, and they're only one source!) so it can't be my connection. I guess it's their software, or our computers, but whatever it is, it's terrible.If you buy this, plan on being able to use the free stuff after a lot of pain and synching and frustration, which is great and the kids love it, but also plan on a lot of misery and work if you're going to load a lot of (expensive!) downloadable content.It's not just my computer, we had trouble on my husband's laptop.It also goes through batteries really fast. You might want to buy some stock in a battery manufacturer if you get one of these.My kids do love it. It's like camping. Fun for kids, not so much for Mom and Dad, who end up doing all the work.They should give these away free and make their money on the downloadable content. It would give them an incentive to make it easier to download and I'd love to spend the $100 on books and games.The potential is not as advertised, unless you're very rich and have a computer that syncs up with their website. It's nice, but the downloadable content costs so much, and is such a hassle to download, that the future potential is almost nonexistent for us, especially since I'm not likely to pay to download content if there's a very good chance it won't sync up.So for the toy we have now, free content safely downloaded, I give high marks. For what it's supposed to be, and could be but isn't, and should be, I adjust my opinion downward.I guess it's a great gift for other people's kids. Don't expect them to like you very much afterwards, though :)
summary: Fun for kids, not so much for parents

reviewText: I played this with my 8 year old and 6 year old. They seemed to really enjoy it. The rules were easy enough to follow. Each player chooses a friends card (features an assortment of friends) and a presents card (features an assortment of presents). You are then each dealt five smaller cards which have the friends and presents on them. Your job is to match the little cards to the presents and friends on your large cards. The leftovers go in the middle of the board. Now it is time to match using a variety of methods including everyone pass a card to the right and digging through the face up pile for a card you need.We had fun. I'm not sure how much educational value there is for older kids. I also didn't love that the focus was get these awesome presents and it is the greatest day ever. Having friends over sure, but lots of presents? I'm sure others will think I'm too picky, but I'm trying to not raise materialistic kids. The focus on gifts is probably the main reason I don't love this game.

reviewText: My two-year-old is obsessed with my digital camera. He loves to take pictures and videos and then watch himself. Unfortunately, I'm a little nervous letting him handle an expensive digital camera. This Fisher-Price-Kid-Tough Camera is the perfect solution to my problem. It's definitely durable enough to take the drops and bumps that will inevitably take place. It's easy for him to use. It didn't take long for him to figure out how to take a picture. The See Yourself feature is fantastic. He loves watching himself on the screen.CONS:*It is SUPER easy to delete pictures and videos on this camera, so if your little angel takes a great picture you may want to upload it as soon as possible. I think my son had just as much fun deleting pictures as he did taking them.*It does NOT include a USB cable, so keep that in mind. They're not very expensive, but with the price of this camera, I wish one would have been included.All in all, it's a great little camera for little ones. It's easy to use, durable, and my son really enjoys using it. Picture quality is decent, the images on the view screen are not as clear as those on my own camera, but they definitely get the job done. As a mom, it's great to have my own camera back again :-) Everyone is happy.
summary: A great hands-on camera for little ones

reviewText: My daughter has a LeapPad and has recently taken the jump into reading, so I was excited to try this out. We generally really like the Leap products, and even have a few of the movies :) However, it seems that maybe this one falls a bit short.The stylus reading with this ebook is a little rough - it can be difficult to have the whole word read out loud. Sometimes you get just a letter or a blend instead. Repeatedly. It's not terrible, but can be a bit frustrating for an emerging reader who is trying to figure something out. The story itself is cute, but it isn't very long and it really isn't very interactive. Not as much as one would expect from an electronic story for kids, anyway. My daughter has now had this about 6 months or so, and I can count on one hand the times she has voluntarily sat down to "read" this. However, she has pulled out her Tag Reader several times and even asked for more books for her birthday.In short, I like the idea, but it seems to be lacking in the execution department. These things are too expensive to not end up with something that kids will want to play with/read more than a handful of times.

reviewText: This board game tests your consumer knowledge of popular brands, slogans, jingles and taglines.  Apparently, I watch too much TV because I knew more of these than I care to admit.The basic premise is you are asked a question, and if you get it right, you advance along the board.  If you get it wrong, the next player has the opportunity to answer.  The questions are a mix of products from both the past and current day.  The box lists for children 12 and up, but honestly, my 12-yr-old never heard of any of the products that were popular in my day, so it's probably a game that should be reserved for adults.Is it fun?  I thought so!  Keep in mind it's a simple game that doesn't involve any strategic planning, outwitting your opponents, or lucky rolls of the dice.  It's just a trivia game about consumer products.  I enjoyed walking down memory lane and laughing about some of the products from my youth.

reviewText: We purchased this set to go with the Melissa and Doug easel, and the only complaint I have (and it's a minor one) is that it only comes with one (blue) dry erase marker.  Beyond that, the items in this set have exceeded my expectations.  First, the paints really are washable (note--my kids paint outside, so I can't comment on whether or not the paint comes out of carpeting).  The paint is just the right consistency--not too thick, not too thin--and the colors look just as vibrant when they dry as when they are wet.  The best part is that the paint washes right off of my kids' hands. The paint cups are genius!  I love the inverted lids that help decrease mess and also keep the paintbrushes in place.  Clean-up is so simple--I just rinse the brushes under cold running water and wipe the cups and lids with a damp paper towel, and they're clean!  Any splatters of paint that land in the paint tray or on the whiteboard can also just be wiped away with a damp paper towel.  Snap the storage lids on top of the paint cups, and the paint doesn't dry out in between art sessions. The chalk is colorful and sturdy--if it can stand up to my three-year-old, who tends to be hard on her crayons and sidewalk chalk, it can stand up to anyone!  The included eraser is also of very good quality.  This is a great set and I'm very glad that we purchased it.  When we run out of paint and chalk, I will definitely buy Melissa and Doug replacements!I am editing my review several days later to include an additional comment regarding the chalk.  Another reviewer mentioned that the chalk creates a lot of dust.  Our experience thus far has been that the green chalk, in particular, creates an amazing amount of dust. I've had to teach my kids to clap the eraser after they erase their drawings, otherwise the next time they go to use the eraser, it just smears green chalk dust around on the chalkboard.  I'm not changing my overall rating for this set, though, since it is still a great value.  We just may end up purchasing another brand of chalk when our Melissa and Doug chalk runs out.

I've had to teach my kids to clap the eraser after they erase their drawings, otherwise the next time they go to use the eraser, it just smears green chalk dust around on the chalkboard. I'm not changing my overall rating for this set, though, since it is still a great value. We just may end up purchasing another brand of chalk when our Melissa and Doug chalk runs out.

reviewText: First things first - you need an iOS device for this thing.  All you get in the box is a pencil-shaped capacitive stylus.  If you search the Apple App Store with the title of this product, you can download the app and take it for a test drive before you purchase this product...if you do purchase the product, you can unlock the app to get the full version (or I guess you can pay for the full version via an in-app purchase, but then you don't get the fun pencil...).  Really, what you will see here is a review of the app, not so much the pencil device.This is for a three-going-on-four year old who is able to draw some individual letters but doesn't really get what they mean yet.  He really took to the app quite well.  It's easy enough that after I set up a profile for him (the app allows for individual profiles so parents can track the progress of multiple users) he can launch and start things up on his own.  As for usage, the features are friendly graphics and dialogue, and my son is able to follow along with no help from me.  He does have trouble holding the overlarge pencil though...small hands, giant pencil, uncomfortable kid.  I did have a smaller capacitive stylus handy that he used instead, but then that all kind of defeats the purpose of buying this product...just download and unlock the app, I guess.Anyway, another thing to note is that the app itself seems large-ish.  I installed this on a 1st Gen iPad and it took quite a while to download and install.  Presumably it would be faster on a later generation iPad, but if you're putting this app on an older one prepare to devote 20 minutes or so to the process.Lastly, the actual exercises being done are similar, if not identical, to the writing exercises in other LeapPad products.  One of the older kids has a LeapPad device (looks like an iPad but with an attached stylus) and the exercises were very much the same.  I'd say if you already have a LeapPad, this product would likely be redundant.Overall though, my son received great value from this product and app.  I even caught my seven year old playing with it.  It seems fun for them - quite happy with the product, all considered.

reviewText: Please check the comments if you're looking for a link to view the complete LeapPad App Center library. Thanks for the sharing the link!My 6-year-old has had the original Leapster since he was 3. It has always been one of his favorite toys. When he was 3, 4 and even 5 before starting Kindergarten, I thought the educational value of the Leapster software was fantastic. He was starting to read and write and was doing basic math before he even entered Kindergarten and I attribute that in part to his love of his Leapster. That said, technology has changed over the last several years and being older, he has access to a wider variety of learning tools. I can't help but compare the LeapPad to the iPod touch. For an educational device, many parents would overlook the iPod touch because it's viewed more as a multimedia device for pre-teens and up. I've had an iPod touch and iPhone for 3 years (and more recently an iPad), and I am an avid app store addict. I can easily list dozens of quality apps available of the hundreds of thousands in iTunes that offer similar educational value to LeapFrog's offerings. If you're wondering where Innotab stands in all of this.. It doesn't! I wrote a lengthy review on our experiences with the Innotab as well and why I think it fails miserably as an educational device but excels as a durable, kid-friendly media player at a price point that can't be beat. Check out my profile and review if you're interested on the full comparison. I won't mention it again here because I don't believe it's in the same educational class as LeapPad by a long shot.LeapPad vs. iPod Touch-----------------------1. Price - Clearly LeapPad wins initially being about half the cost of the iPod. Just remember, you get what you pay for! In the long term, the iPod touch actually comes out ahead in this area. Leapfrog App Center apps are generally grouped in three price categories. There are $7.50 selections which seem to be the most basic games and the "no frills" e-books. The cartridge "expansions" are also in this price range. I purchased the Cars 2 expansion for the cartridge at this price and it appears to have added 3 new tracks. Quite expensive. Then you have the $10 games and videos which offer a little more content but many of the videos are available for streaming if you have a Netflix or Prime subscription. To give you a idea, the Word World videos are $10 and contain 2 full length episodes. Then you jump up to the $20 bracket and this is where the Ultra e-books are. Ultra means the pages are much more animated and more interactive than the basic e-books. Also, to my surprise, there are a number of games within the e-book. I downloaded the Cars 2 deluxe e-book and it is very cute and the ability to sound out the words in addition to having a built in dictionary for a few words in the book has value for sure, but $20 value? iTunes has countless "deluxe e-books" with these kinds of features at $2 or less. There is even a Cars 2 book that is very similar to the deluxe e-book and I paid $0.99 for it. So far, I've put about $220 into the LeapPad, including 4 cartridge games and 3 app center cards (two of which I got here on Black Friday for $14) and in total, we now have 10 games (including the free downloads you get for purchasing it) and an expansion for a cartridge game. I could have easily gotten a good number of quality educational apps and games for the iPod touch for this same value. It goes downhill from there. For each cartridge game purchased, you could have gotten 25 $0.99 games from iTunes.2. Memory - I had to revise this section of my review as I didn't give LeapPad a fair shake the first time around. By today's digital standards, 2GB of storage sounds like nothing, but after doing the math, I added up the size of ALL games, e-books, ultra e-books, expansions, creativity apps, flash cards in the App Center and you could easily fit every single one of them on the LeapPad's internal storage. This includes the built in apps and all 8 of the cartridge games that are offered in digital format (LeapSchool Reading, Pet Pals 2, Dora, Globe: Earth Adventures, Mr. Pencil, Ni-Hao Kai-lan and both SpongeBob titles). There's even a little room left for a few videos! Nice!! I can't imagine you'd ever want everything in the App Center, but if you did, you could have them! Just be sure to leave room for your child's photos, videos and stories that they create. Now for the iPod, they start at 8GB. You get four times the memory for twice the price. After some consideration, I feel that this is a bit like comparing apples to oranges. LeapPad is very self-contained, and given the fact that it can hold everything available (minus the videos) it makes the size of it's storage a moot point.3. Camera - The pictures taken with the LeapPad are passable but definitely not print quality. The iPod touch actually has a fairly decent camera that can take beautiful pictures in good light. The LeapPad also lacks a front camera which makes taking pictures of yourself impossible without the help of a mirror, though it offers a "timer" that tells you to turn the LeapPad around so the camera is facing you and hold it til you hear the shutter sound. It's a nice attempt, but my several attempts never got a centered picture of my face. Not even close! My son has several free apps on his iPod that change the picture in real time and he has spent many hours looking at himself and I and our dogs with these apps. On the flip side, your child probably won't care about the loss in picture quality! My son has spent just as much time with my mom's camera on her Nintendo DS which is far worse than the LeapPad's camera.4. Screen - I was actually surprised when I compared the two. The LeapPad appears so much bigger, but it's screen size is only about 1.5" taller and .5" wider. Bigger isn't always better with these types of devices and it shows. This is where it becomes clear that the LeapPad, as amazing as it is, is still just a toy. The picture is nice and clear for playing the games, but it just can't hold a candle to the iPod's beautifully crisp retina display.5. Performance - The LeapPad is designed for very young children, and as such it's built around durability, not so much around amazing eye-popping graphics. The graphics themselves are fine for this type of device, but the games feel a little jerky at times. In the writing game, you have to make fairly slow strokes because the processor simply can't keep up with fast motions. The line you draw is a second or two behind your actual drawing of the line. This is honestly my biggest complaint about the LeapPad. It should at least be able to keep up! This is annoying when we are used to playing games on iPods and iPads with silky smooth performance and instant response. The load times are annoying as well but the Innotab suffers this same malady.6. Durability - The iPod loses here because though they are very well made, they are not designed for small children and they will suffer scratches and even breaks if handled roughly enough. However, my son received his iPod last Christmas when he was 5 years old, and he isn't overly cautious with his toys but I have never had an issue with him not handling the iPod properly. Would I have given him an iPod when he was 3 years old? Not likely. His Leapster held on through many drops, throws and stomps and I have no doubt that the LeapPad will hold up just as well. If your little one isn't yet at the age to understand how to handle their toys with care, you absolutely want the LeapPad.7. Compatibility - Here's where I get annoyed with LeapFrog. We have had a Leapster since the original, and at 25 bucks a piece, the games are by no means cheap. We have a few dozen games and most of them were purchased used from eBay because I thought it was ridiculous to spend so much for a game for a 3-year-old. Then along came the Leapster 2. Thankfully, our old games still worked. Many games, though, came out with "new" versions for the Leapster 2. The games were the same but in order to access the "extra online content" you had to buy the new version of the game, which was a joke, in my opinion. I never replaced our original games with Leapster 2 versions because I didn't see the so-called "content" being worth handing over another 25 bucks per game. Fast forward to last year with the release of the Leapster Explorer and they have all new games that are NOT compatible with previous versions of the Leapster. This was very disappointing, especially since many of the games were remakes of the old games yet again. Now we have the LeapPad and the Leapster Explorer games ARE compatible with the LeapPad but in another generation or two, I have no doubt these cartridges will also become obsolete. This is where I'm enjoying the new technology. Leapster Explorer was the hot handheld last year, and if you put your money into apps for it, they are compatible with the LeapPad as well. Yay! I'm hoping LeapFrog sticks with this format and always ensures their older digital content is compatible with future models. Where does the iPod come into play with all of this? Everything you purchase from iTunes, be it apps, games, books, movies, music, etc, is completely compatible with all past and future models of the iPod touch, iPhone and iPad. And you don't have to carry around cartridges that just love to get lost in car seats and at Grandma's house and in the dog's mouth. Though to be fair, a good number of the cartridge games are available in digital format from the App Center, saving you from at least some of the hassle of cartridges. I like to feel like my money is well spent, and I feel totally ripped off with the high cost of the Leapfrog cartridges. I never buy them at full price and will only purchase them when they are on sale. Even then, I feel they have yet to hit the sweet spot. If their software was just a little cheaper, no parent would have an excuse not to buy a LeapPad for their kids.8. App selection - The iTunes library of 200,000+ apps easily beats LeapPad's 100+ combined apps, games, books and videos, and the vast majority of apps available in iTunes are FAR cheaper than LeapPad's selections. Most of the educational apps I've downloaded for my son for his iPod (and our shared iPad) were either free or 99 cents. iTunes has an entire section of educational apps and many of them are always free. If it's not free, chances are someday it will be free or 99 cents and you get far more bang for your buck with these apps than you do paying 10 bucks and up for the games in the Leapfrog app store. The drawback is, you have to sift through a lot of junk apps in iTunes to find the gems. LeapFrog doesn't offer junk and therefore saves you the trouble of trying to hunt down the good apps. Convenience has a price, however!9. Convenience - Portability is a big deal to me. My son and I travel several times a year and they are usually very long road trips. I need something to keep him busy for many many hours while he's stuck in his seat. The iPod fits in my pocket in a pinch and in my purse the rest of the time. He can even carry it in his own pants pocket. The LeapPad is significantly larger, which is great for tiny hands, but makes it more difficult to store, especially when you consider that you have to take all the cartridges along with you. Aside from portability, ease of use also comes into play. If you want to download content to your iPod, you simply have to be in range of a wireless network, either your home network or any number of free wireless locations such as Panera or McDonald's and most hotels offer free or cheap wifi. You can use app store cards or have purchases billed directly to your credit card. With the LeapPad, in addition to still needing access to a wireless network, you need to have access to a PC. Not just any PC, but the PC you have the Leapfrog Connect software installed on. If this is your home desktop PC, you won't be downloading anything new while you're on the road. If it's on your laptop, you may fare better but it's still a pain in the rear to have to do everything through the PC. I understand adding wifi to the LeapPad would have added to the cost, so it's the trade off you have to make for choosing a less expensive device. That said, finding quality educational apps on iTunes means you have to sift through some stuff that's less than great. Thankfully, iTunes has a huge community and most apps will have reviews from other parents. You don't have this same convenience with Leapfrog app purchases. I was surprised that LeapFrog doesn't offer any kind of rating system in their App Center. Even Vtech's Learning Lodge has a rating system!10. Battery - The iPod touch has a built in rechargeable battery than can be charged either via wall outlet or USB port on your computer. The LeapPad, however, uses 4 AA batteries. Be prepared to replace the batteries at least once a day initially. You will absolutely want to pick up a good set of rechargeable batteries. I highly recommendSanyo NEW 1500 eneloop 4 Pack AAA Ni-MH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries. I have been using them for 5 years and still have my original set. They run about $10 for 4 AA batteries, and they are well worth it. Any rechargeable battery charger will charge these though you can buy an eneloop charger as well. What sets these batteries apart from other brands is they have an extremely low discharge rate. With typical rechargeable batteries, you're going to run into the issue of them losing charge while sitting on the shelf waiting for use. Eneloop claims these batteries retain 75% of their charge after 3 years of no use and I completely believe it. I had a spare set that hadn't been used in at least a year and we got over 4 hours of use out of them before we had to switch to a freshly charged set. I can't recommend them enough for parents who have a lot of battery powered toys, especially battery hogs like the LeapPad!It sounds like I'm tearing LeapPad apart, but I really do think it's a great educational toy for the appropriate age group. If money isn't an object and you want real, educational entertainment for your child, look no further. I just feel the age estimate on the box of 4-9 is not at all accurate. I don't see anything here that will hold the attention of a 8 or 9-year-old and I was really disappointed with this as I thought it was something that could grow with my son for a few more years. Though if your child is under the age of 7, and especially in the 3-5 year old range, there are many great entertaining opportunities to learn here. These kids may not quite be old enough for the responsibility of owning a more expensive device, but they will really benefit from the high quality build and durability of the LeapPad. If you don't mind doing a little detective work to find the educational gems in iTunes and have children able to handle an iPod responsibly, I would hands down recommend the iPod touch as a much better value, fantastic portability and a device that can truly grow with your child into the pre-teen years and beyond.

reviewText: I usually use scissors that are open and glide it through wrapping paper , rather than open and close the scissors.  When I saw this product, I thought it would be perfect for me.  It is (almost).  It is shaped like a toothbrush handle with a padded grip.  The blade is safely contained within the top of the handle so there is no chance of accidentally cutting oneself.  To cut, you insert the paper into the opening, which is shaped like a shallow "V" and then push.  Once it starts cutting, you can glide through paper like butter!The reason I didn't give the product 4 stars is because it didn't do great on thin paper.  It would not start cutting and ended up crumpling up the paper.  I ended up either completely crumpling the edge or tearing the paper.  However, once I got it started, it cut beautifully.  With thicker wrapping paper, it worked perfectly.As of today (after all my Christmas wrapping), the blade was still razor sharp.  I do wonder, however, how long that will last, but it definitely made it through the season without a problem.Overall, I really liked this product.  It was made for people like me who like cutting paper in a straight line.

reviewText: This is a really silly family board game/action game. The game play is simple. Read a card, do the action. The next player has to repeat the previous action(s) and do their new action. This goes round and round, repeating the things in sequence, until someone messes up or forgets what to do.The things that must be done range from actions without sounds, to actions with sounds to just sounds or words spoken. Examples are to act and make sounds like a bat, say "Boo!", stomp your feet on the floor, snore, make a thumbs-up sign without a sound, and smack your lips and make the sound.The game description mentions a time limit but the game does not come with a timer of any sort and the directions say to make up your own time. That is tricky since our game had as many as 12 actions being done in a row. We didn't do the timing part.The scoring and who is the winner is a bit chancy, the punishment for the one who messes up is to roll the die and go backwards the number of spaces they rolled.This game is really, really silly and some adults may not like doing these wacky things with their kids but if that is the case maybe they need this game to loosen them up. My boys aged 11 and 8 really loved the game including seeing their parents acting like fools, such as when my husband crawled on the floor on his stomach and made sounds like a crocodile. Oh boy.I'm not sure how teens would like to play this game with each other. I can imagine my boys playing this with their friends right now (if their friends were willing) and cracking up at what they were doing, so long as everyone had good sportsmanship and didn't make fun of the kids who messed up.Our game didn't go on too long, so I didn't get to the point where the game was going to drive me insane if I continued.The game maker says this games goes to age 99. I cannot imagine adults playing this with each other unless they changed it into a drinking game of some sort or were playing under the influence of alcohol, which could be quite hysterical actually.I'm rating this game a 5 for fun and overall, because it is a good clean fun family game that the kids think is hilarious, and because I believe that more good board games are needed on the market and because I think all families should play board games and card games with each other as it builds connections between family members.I'm rating this a 4 for educational because it helps children learn to pay attention, sequencing and helps practice memory work. A child who does not look and listen closely and focus will have a hard time at this game. The skills that this game practices are good for all children to be able to do and will help them in school.
summary: Silly Family Board and Action Game, Worth Playing

reviewText: Singin' Cookie Monster is an adorable doll. At about one foot in height, Cookie is small enough to snuggle with little ones. He is decked out in a cookie decorated shirt, blue pants and fabric sneakers. His clothing feels polyester, but I think that is for ease of cleaning. Cookie himself is soft shag, much like other plush Cookie Monster dolls. He has only three parts of plastic pieces that are rather hard: the microphone, his eyes, and the battery pack within his torso.You get Cookie to speak and sing by pulling his microphone in front of his mouth. The audio is clear and quiet. There is no volume control, so it's a good thing that it is quiet. There are two modes to choose from on the battery pack, "on" and "try me." I could not get him to sing in the "on" mode, only the "try me" mode, which seems odd to me. Also, the singing stops in the middle of the song, so you have to pull his arm again to finish it. "On" allows for much more speaking, while "try me" is reduced to singing and a couple of snippets of words. These short bursts of speech may be a good thing, as this doll will not keep singing long after he is prompted. And prompting him with his arm seems to help against accidental outbursts.A small instruction sheet is easy to understand and even includes lyrics. Also, this is the most open friendly packaging ever! Paper ties and easy to loosen and remove string made the doll accessible within minutes without scissors or hurting myself--a major accomplishment for a boxed toy.Overall, it's pretty cute, but does not say or sing many things. For your little one, it will probably be enough. I have not tried him with Elmo, but maybe that is how this toy is most effective during playtime.

reviewText: Funny Bunny is a simple & entertaining game that should appeal to little ones and which manages to be fun for parents & older kids too.  The gameboard is a plastic hill with a spiraling path of spots leading to the center, where a protruding carrot awaits and marks the end of the path - and victory for the first player whose bunny gamepiece reaches it.  This carrot also serves another purpose, as it can be twisted to open up spots on the gameboard.  If your gamepiece has landed on the spot that opens up with the twist of the carrot, it falls through and disappears from the board and is eliminated from play.  This unique means of eliminating player pieces is what puts the "fun" in Funny Bunny.Gameplay is simple, with each player taking turns drawing a card which either advances that player's piece forward 1, 2, or 3 spaces or which has the player give the carrot a twist.  The suggested age range of 4+ is appropriate, though we've found that on those occasions when we play this to include our almost-four-year-old daughter in playtime the rest of the family enjoys it too, including 7 year old big brother and mom and dad.  Twisting the carrot and anticipating which bunny will drop through the hole and out of sight is actually quite enjoyable.  There isn't much strategy involved, though players have a small amount of decision-making in choosing which of their own 4 bunnies to move during their turn.  Little ones will use basic skills like turn-taking and counting, and will also use a bit of their motor skills when twisting the carrot.Overall this is a cute game that little ones will enjoy and which provides some fun for the older members of the family too.  Make no mistake - this is a simple game aimed at young kids, but the novelty of the disappearing bunnies is clever and gives this one broader appeal than other games aimed at preschoolers.  The board and pieces are cute and sturdy too, and I expect they'll last through as many kids as you need them to.  Overall a fine choice for gaming families that want to include their preschoolers and offer some fun to the older players too.

reviewText: This is classic monopoly with three changes.First, the prices are in the millions.  Basically, $100 = one million.  There might have been some modest tweaks to the prices as well, but generally speaking Hasboro seems to have just converted the old prices to the new scale.  Second, there are modernized tokens like a cell phone and skateboard, and the old tokens (or at least most of them) are gone.  Not much need to comment on these first two changes, you can form your own opinion without more info.Third, and this is the big one, everything that previously involved money is now done with the player's individual debit cards and a calculator type device.  The device and credit cards actually work surprisingly well, but the negatives outweight the positives:(1) the possibility for errors to go undetected seems larger than using the fake cash, and a battery failure or accidental reset of the device could potentially KILL a game you spent hours on.  Again, it works well, but the risk has to be bigger than accidentally knocking the board on the floor;(2) The device takes any learning of math out of it for the kids.  Leaving aside learning, it is difficult to watch over correct use of the device, making it MUCH harder for a child to be the banker at all;(3)  Time is a wash.  Leaving aside the obviously easier set-up and clean up using the device, as far as actually using it during the game, it is not easier than using the fake cash, and in some instances it might take a smidge more time (when one player is paying another and two of the debit cards must be used);(4)  Its rather easy to forget how much cash you have, making money management harder;(5)  No convenient way to do the penalties go into Free Parking variant.(6)  Annoying Factor:  Finally, and I admit this is purely subjective, but I just find it (more) annoying to be the banker and use the device.Conclusion:  There is nothing terrible about this version.  Its still monopoly.  However, I think the chance of screwing up a long game due to a battery failure, errors or an accidental reset really outweighs the slight time savings, if any, associated with using the debit cards.  This is especially true if you were hoping that Monopoly would help your kids with their math.

reviewText: This playset is what I'd expect from Fisher-Price: it will hold up to plenty of play and there are plenty of pieces and things to do. I'm holding back from a 5-star rating because there's nothing truly outstanding about it, but it's a solid pick for Mike the Knight fans. Another nice thing is that this isn't too show/character specific; children can enjoy this as a generic knight and castle set without being a fan of the show.The zipline is a fun addition and pretty functional. I like that Mike can actually sit on the horse. The catapult works well and yet the "rock" is too light to cause any real harm. Several things like this means the set has potential for lots of fun. I have only a few minor complaints. There would be much more potential for interactive play with more human figures included; I find this is a common issue with playsets and suspect it's intentional in hopes customers will buy more figures. Then there are details like the fact that it's hard to fit Gallahad (the horse) in the spot with the hay and trough. Overall it's a pretty good choice and should be lots of fun for many children in the 2-4 age range.

reviewText: We haven't had much luck with educational toys -- since all they seem to teach our son is that learning isn't fun.  It's just the opposite with the Leapfrog Tag.  He loves to run the pen over the words, hear the sounds, and play the games -- all by himself.  He is enthralled with the Spiderman and Scooby-Doo books (which I bought separately).  What is he learning?  Frankly, I don't much care.  Five year olds deserve to have toys that they like that don't teach them a darn thing.  But I do think he's growing to understand what words look like since he moves the pen to each new word confidently, and that's one of the first steps in being a confident reader.

reviewText: Dusty Crophopper RC plane is a cute, fun toy.  After my granddaughter saw the movie, she was so excited about it that I wanted to get her this toy.  When she saw it, she squealed with delight.  Of course she immediately wanted to play with it, but we soon found it was difficult to play with in the house.  It was nighttime when I gave it to her, so she had to wait until the next day to try it outside.  The reason it's hard to play with in the house is that it needs a lot of space in which to turn and roll, and it really doesn't work that well on carpet, even with a low pile.  It works best on a flat, smooth surface like a kitchen floor, but my kitchen and dining room space is too small and the plane just runs into the furniture.  When we took it outside on the driveway, we had much better results.  However, if the plane runs into any obstacle, like a pebble or twig, it will stop and often flip forward to rest on the propeller.My granddaughter got a kick out of using the controls that fit on her hands.  She isn't quite coordinated enough yet to hold a remote and maneuver it, while also looking at the RC vehicle, and with this remote control, she doesn't have to look at the remote.  She just moves her hands.  She does have to press the button on the right controller with her thumb to make it go forward, but she mastered that pretty quickly.My 2.5 year old grandson also likes Dusty.  He can't really use the remote, but it comes with 3 built-in moves and he really enjoys that.  He also likes to pick Dusty up and pretend to make him fly.Don't forget to pick up 4AA and 2AAA batteries before you give this to a child.  It doesn't come with the batteries and they will be very disappointed if they can't use it right away.  It uses up batteries pretty quickly, but it does have an auto shutoff feature that helps with battery life should the child turn it on and then forget about it.If your child is really into Planes, then I recommend this toy.  If they're not into the movie or haven't seen it, then it may not be as much fun, given the difficulties mentioned above.
summary: Needs large, flat area to play. Not really for in the house play.

reviewText: I am an IT guy so when I saw this I had to get it to test it out. I always like to see how technology is being implemented in kids toys so they are introduced to it early. As a kid I would have loved something like this toy. Slide the ipad in (make sure the protective screen is on it) and turn it on, fire up the special app and you have barnyard magic going on. The kids can interact with the screen using the various toys to plow fields, grow crops, etc. It's pretty slick.So is it work it? The price as of the date I write this is only $19.99, I believe it dropped $10 since I originally got it. Keep in mind though you need to include your own iPad which makes this toy total $419 or so. It's awesome yes, but there is always a risk a kid can be rough and your iPad could get damaged. That being said, I like it but I would personally pass on it. I would love to see this toy cost $50 or $75 and include the screen on it already. Yes that increases cost, but what if your kid wants to play with the toy while you are using your tablet? It's a great concept, I'm excited by what is coming along but at this time I can't justify the risk versus the cost.
summary: Great concept, decent price as long as you have an ipad laying around.

reviewText: We're in the stage where we don't have as much energy as we did when we had little children so this is a welcome addition to our "keep the grandbaby and young visitors entertained" collection.The grandbaby is a bit young for it but that will soon change. In the meantime, friends have had grandchildren and they are eager to visit.I prefer toys which leave plenty to young ones' imaginations. This does, allowing older babies and toddlers to release their Wheelies vehicles filled with Little People riders down a long ramp. They can see what happens, then experiment a bit and then watch the results the next  time around.There are lights, sounds, and all sorts of moving parts. There is also a ticket booth, mirror, food stand, movable flags,and more. And, of course, the Wheelies cars (two in this set) and their passengers.If you decide to purchase this, do keep in mind the fact that it does take up some space, being over 2 feet tall. But make room for it if you possibly can. There are so many attention-grabbing activities in this set that  toddlers and even babies as young as 14 months remain (miraculously) in place long enough for parents or grandparents to sit back and take a breath.It sure beats running after an active toddler darting from one thing to another. I've raised our children. I now take a nap several times a week. I also have some visitors who don't always keep track of their children as well as I'd wish.So I am almost as much in love with the Loops n' Swoops Amusement Park as the little ones. This set - and some well placed baby gates- help keep things as stress-free as I could possibly imagine when toddlers hit our house.I'm not a total grump and spoil sport. I do like to get down on the floor and play with the kids sometimes. I just have a harder time getting up than I used to. Knees creak. Bones groan. So I'm glad this often needs minimal adult assistance for kids to enjoy it.You do need to have AA batteries on hand so stock up ahead of time on those. On warm days you can take this outside and on cold ones you may keep winter boredom from turning into utter stir crazy insanity. I remember those very l..o..n..g winter days.If you're anticipating guests with very young children for Thanksgiving, Christmas or any occasion in between, seriously consider purchasing the Wheelies Amusement Park.A super contender for a birthday or Christmas gift for some lucky recipient, too.
summary: One of the few toys we've used which keep even the youngest ones entertained

reviewText: This Fisher-Price barnyard farm toy set is a large scale version of the FP classics. We also have the little play and go boxed farm set that has been around for decades, consider this just a less portable version of that...with sounds!What I LIKE about this toy: It was easy to set up, just snap in place and screw in two screws and you're good to go! It came with batteries and sounds, working right out of the box, which is nice. It's a good set up, with the stalls the cow & horse can rest in, your child can slide/throw animals down the silo and it makes a clever noise, and you can set up a fenced corral. It's a fun toy to have around to play with your toddler, sure enough. The gates make barnyard noises and a few other sounds. Especially if your child is into the farm scene thing, this might very well be a hit.What I DON'T LIKE about this toy, there are a few things: I feel like they could have thrown in an extra animal, or two, for this price set. I see the older version also included a pig and a goat. This newer set only includes the horse, cow, and sheep. The chicken is stuck in place and just spins around while clicking. Oh, and there's the little farmer who my kids couldn't care less about--it's all about the animals! So I really wish they'd included a couple more. This large of a farm, and only 3 movable animals?I also found some of the sounds, particularly the songs, to be very annoying. Sure, this is a personal opinion thing, but Fisher-Price likes to add these uber cutesy sing-a-long songs to their toys. We've had the singing teapot, the singing purse, the singing farm now. My kids don't care about the songs, they don't like the songs, they have never sung along, they serve no purpose other than to annoy. I find myself wishing they'd kept the sounds to classic barnyard noises, or just good old tunes like "The Farmer in the Dell" without the tiny little fairy voice singing along loudly. Again, personal opinion, maybe some folks like this, but around here we don't.So, overall I'd say I have mixed feelings about this toy. It's cute and fun, especially for the farm-loving toddler. My girls, 5 & 2, get to visit their grandparent's farm on a regular basis so they get a kick out of playing with these farm toys too. The animals especially, they are very fond of (which is why I wish FP had included one or two more!) If you're shopping for such a child for a gift and this one appeals to you then I say sure, why not? There's nothing wrong with it, I just felt it could be better. I do think there are other farm sets--even in the Fisher-Price line--that are a little better than this one.
summary: Fun enough--could they give us MORE animals and fewer annoying songs though?

reviewText: My eight-year-old daughter has been a Polly Pocket fan for several years now so she was super excited to receive this playset. The set up out of the box was really easy and I think this playset makes for a great summer toy. The little boat can be attached to the rest of the 'yacht' and looks like one big yacht, but it can also be opened up to reveal a sort of island retreat with two attached plastic palm trees and several accessories such as a deck chair, a BBQ grill that flips, a beach umbrella, and little fashion accessories for the one blonde-haired Polly doll that comes with this set. If you have a Polly fan at home that has other Polly playsets, the dolls can be used to buddy up with this Polly doll (we actually managed to find a couple of dolls ,other deck chairs, and beach umbrellas from other summer-themed playsets so that Polly and friends could throw a great beach party).There's another bonus to this playset - the smaller speedboat can be easily detached from the front of the yacht and when you push the little button, Polly will perform some cool water ski flips! It is a fun playset, perfect for the summer! Note: There are some tiny accessories that come with this playset so I would recommend it for ages 5 and up as the smaller items could pose a choking hazard.
summary: Super summer fun for Polly fans
